items.title: Earth has a New Moon
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN:

Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. 

The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. 


While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... 

The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

items.title: Bitcoin Drops to $56,085, a Two-Year Low, in Worst Month Since 2022
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Seven days ago Slashdot reported Bitcoin had plummeted 24% in just 46 days. Since then it's dropped another 9.4%, falling to $56,085 by Friday night, its lowest price in over two years. "It has lost more than half its value since reaching a peak above $126,000 in October 2025," reports Bloomberg, noting it's now worth less than when Donald Trump first took office in January of 2025. 

Yahoo Finance reports:

At its current price, the digital coin is down more than 20% so far in November, putting it on pace for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, according to Yahoo Finance data. That would be bitcoin's eighth-worst month since Yahoo Finance's daily records began tracking the digital asset in September 2014... 

US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also added to the selling pressure. So far this month, net investors have withdrawn roughly $3.5 billion, according to asset manager Farside Investors, which tracks the product flows. That includes $582 million in outflows on Thursday alone.
 

"Bitcoin's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the 'digital gold' market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned," writes CNBC. 

They note Bitcoin "is on pace for its seventh-straight weekly loss for the first time since May 2022, according to CNBC data."

Financial markets are chaotic. So chaotic, even, that many economists and investors believe market trends to be the product of ‘random walks’ and that prices cannot be predicted (see generally Malkiel). But randomness shouldn't be worrisome. In fact, random price movements can be good. Gaussian random walk, an assumption used by an options pricing model called Black-Scholes, treats intervals of an asset’s price over time as independent variables. By doing so, the changes in price over time, or the returns of an asset, are assumed to be normally distributed. Otherwise stated, “If transactions are fairly uniformly spread across time, and if the number of transactions per day, week, or month is very large, then the Central Limit Theorem leads us to expect that these price changes will have normal or Gaussian distributions” (Fama, 399). When an asset's returns are normally distributed, the probabilities of those returns are known. Knowing these probabilities can give investors a reliable framework accounting for the risk of holding said asset. When it comes to bitcoin, much has been said about how risky it is. The purpose of this article is to explore how to frame risk and to test how well traditional assumptions, implicit in derivatives pricing, apply to bitcoin.

items.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.
 
The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED.
 
"We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

items.title: Setting Up AWS Control Tower? These SCP and Networking Mistakes Can Cost You Hours
items.author: Tokarev Artem
items.content:
Most landing-zone guides stop after "click Set up landing zone". This one keeps going. By the end, you will have a working multi-account AWS environment where every account has one job, the rules are enforced by Service Control Policies, and the network is owned by one account and shared with the others. Each rule is tested from the command line, so you can prove it holds.

Everything here was built in a real organization, including the parts that went wrong: an SCP that broke DNS, an "allow list" SCP that allowed everything, and a RAM share that failed for 40 minutes. The fixes are part of the steps and are collected in the Troubleshooting section.

This is part 1 of a series. Part 2 sets up the Build account (CodeCommit, ECR with cross-account pull, and CodeBuild inside the shared VPC), and part 3 runs the application on ECS in Dev and Production.

Seven accounts, grouped into Organizational Units (OUs), each with one responsibility:

  • (Root OU) owns AWS Organizations, Control Tower, IAM Identity Center, SCPs. Must not: run workloads.
  • (Security OU) owns security tooling and findings (Config aggregator, GuardDuty, Security Hub).
  • (Security OU) owns central CloudTrail and Config logs.
  • (Infrastructure OU) owns all VPCs, subnets, routes, NAT and internet gateways. Must not: run applications or CI/CD.
  • (Deployments OU) owns source repository, CodeBuild, CodePipeline, ECR. Must not: own networking, run applications.
  • (Workloads OU) owns the application in the dev environment. Must not: own networking, build or push images.
  • (Workloads OU) owns the application in production. Must not: own networking, build or push images.

The "must not" rules matter as much as ownership: each one becomes a Deny statement in an SCP, so it holds even for an administrator inside that account.

What you will have at the end:

  • An organization with five OUs and seven accounts, governed by Control Tower (section 4).
  • Single sign-on to every account through IAM Identity Center, with no IAM users or access keys anywhere (section 4).
  • Four deny-based SCPs that enforce each account's job (section 5).
  • Three VPCs owned by the Network account, each shared only with its own environment (section 6).
  • A script that proves all of the above in one run (section 7).
  • The diagram already shows the Build pipeline and the workloads. They are built on this foundation in parts 2 and 3.

2. Why one account per responsibility?

An AWS account is a hard boundary for IAM permissions, billing, service quotas, and the blast radius of mistakes. When dev, prod, networking, and CI/CD share one account, a developer who needs the dev cluster easily ends up with access to production, and costs can only be split with careful tagging. Separate accounts give you these boundaries for free, and OUs let you apply the same rules to a group of accounts at once: every account you add to the Workloads OU later inherits its guardrails.

The design follows one principle, ownership: for any resource, it should be obvious which account owns it and who is allowed to change it. The network belongs to the Network account, images belong to the Build account, and the running application belongs to the workload account. Images are built once and only pulled by Dev and Production, so Production runs exactly what was tested in Dev.

This article builds only Dev and Production. A Staging account can be added later in exactly the same way.

3. Prerequisites and cost

  • An AWS account that is not yet part of an organization. It becomes the management account. Don't use an account that runs workloads.
  • A separate email address for each new account. With Gmail, you can use +aliases such as you+network@gmail.com.
  • AWS CLI v2. All access in this article goes through IAM Identity Center (SSO). We don't create a single IAM user or access key, and the SCPs will even forbid it.
  • About two hours of hands-on time, plus about 35 minutes of waiting while Control Tower sets up.
  • Region: everything runs in eu-central-1 (Frankfurt). Control Tower governs only this Region, and an SCP denies the others. Replace it with your own Region throughout.

Control Tower itself is free, but the services it enables are not. Approximate monthly costs in eu-central-1 for this setup:

Config, CloudTrail, S3 logsA few dollars at this scale

The NAT gateways are almost all of the bill. If you build this only to learn, follow the Cleanup section when you are done, or delete the NAT gateways between sessions.

Control Tower creates the organization structure, the two shared accounts in the Security OU, an organization-wide CloudTrail trail, and AWS Config in every enrolled account. Everything later in this article builds on it.

Before you start: if IAM Identity Center is already enabled in the management account, Control Tower must be set up in the same Region. Choose the home Region carefully. Changing it later means decommissioning the landing zone.

Step 1: Set up the landing zone

Sign in to the management account and open AWS Control Tower → Set up landing zone.

On the first page, choose your home Region and Automatic account enrollment. With automatic enrollment, accounts that join the organization later (and accounts you move between OUs) get the Control Tower baseline and controls without manual enrollment.

On the second page, keep the recommended Sandbox OU. It is a place for experiments with fewer restrictions, and we will also use it to test new SCPs before they reach other OUs.

Next, Control Tower asks for the two shared accounts in the Security OU:

  • Log Archive: stores the CloudTrail and AWS Config logs of every account. I named it "CloudTrail administrator".
  • Audit: aggregates AWS Config data and becomes the delegated administrator for security services. I named it "Aggregator account".
  • You will see these names in the screenshots. Each account needs its own email address. With Gmail, a +alias such as you+audit@gmail.com is enough: mail to it arrives in your normal inbox.

Review the settings and confirm:

The setup takes about 35 minutes. You can follow each step on the landing zone page:

Control Tower created the Security and Sandbox OUs. Create the other three under Root in Control Tower → Organization → Create resources → Create organizational unit: Infrastructure, Deployments, and Workloads. Create them through Control Tower, not the Organizations console, so that they are registered and get the Control Tower controls.

If you expect many workloads, you can nest OUs later, for example Workloads/web and Workloads/ai, and attach different policies to each.

Step 3: Create the accounts

Use Control Tower → Account Factory → Create account for each workload account:

Account Factory provisions accounts one at a time, so creating all four takes a while. When it's done, Control Tower → Organization should show every OU as Registered and every account as Enrolled:

Step 4: Access through IAM Identity Center

Control Tower configures IAM Identity Center. It creates groups such as AWSControlTowerAdmins, AWSSecurityAuditors, and AWSLogArchiveViewers, and permission sets such as AWSAdministratorAccess, AWSPowerUserAccess, and AWSReadOnlyAccess. In every enrolled account, your user gets AWSAdministratorAccess directly, while the AWSControlTowerAdmins group only gets AWSOrganizationsFullAccess. That direct assignment is how I sign in everywhere in this article:

For a team, don't give everyone administrator access. Create groups by role and assign each group only to the accounts it needs:

  • : AWSAdministratorAccess in all accounts
  • : AWSAdministratorAccess in Network
  • : AWSPowerUserAccess in Dev
  • : AWSReadOnlyAccess in Production

In the console: IAM Identity Center → Groups → Create group, then AWS accounts → select the accounts → Assign users or groups → choose the group and the permission set. The same assignment from the CLI:

aws sso-admin create-account-assignment --profile mgmt \
  --instance-arn <identity-center-instance-arn> \
  --target-type AWS_ACCOUNT --target-id <dev-account-id> \
  --permission-set-arn <power-user-permission-set-arn> \
  --principal-type GROUP --principal-id <developers-group-id>

For the command line, add one profile per account to ~/.aws/config, then sign in once with aws sso login --sso-session lz. One sign-in covers all profiles:

[sso-session lz]
sso_start_url = https://<your-portal>.awsapps.com/start
sso_region = eu-central-1
sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access

[profile mgmt]
sso_session = lz
sso_account_id = <management-account-id>
sso_role_name = AWSAdministratorAccess
region = eu-central-1

[profile network]
sso_session = lz
sso_account_id = <network-account-id>
sso_role_name = AWSAdministratorAccess
region = eu-central-1

# ...same for audit, logarchive, build, dev, prod

use the role name that you actually see in the access portal. In my organization the management account has AdministratorAccess while member accounts have AWSAdministratorAccess. A wrong role name fails with "ForbiddenException: No access".

Also check that no AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or AWS_SESSION_TOKEN environment variables are set in your shell. The CLI uses them whenever a command has no --profile, so a single forgotten flag silently runs that command against a completely different account. I had exactly this situation, with keys for an unrelated organization in my shell.

5. Service Control Policies

Service Control Policies (SCPs) are guardrails in AWS Organizations. They define the maximum permissions available to IAM users and roles in the accounts of an OU, regardless of what their IAM policies allow.

We use them to enforce the Region, to block dangerous actions (leaving the organization, disabling security services), to enforce ownership (only the Network account builds connectivity), and to remove risky shortcuts (root user, long-lived access keys). SCPs say "what's possible", IAM policies say "who can do it".

Two rules worth remembering:

  • SCPs never grant permissions. They only limit them.
  • SCPs do not affect the management account, and they do not affect service-linked roles. This is one more reason not to run workloads in the management account.

Allow lists vs. deny lists

There are two ways to write SCPs:

  • Allow list: remove FullAWSAccess from the OU and attach an SCP that allows only specific services.
  • Deny list: keep FullAWSAccess and attach SCPs that explicitly deny what you don't want. A common mistake is an allow-list SCP attached next to FullAWSAccess. SCPs on the same OU are combined, so FullAWSAccess already allows everything and only the "Deny" statements have any effect. I made exactly this mistake in my first version. The Workloads OU policy "allowed only ECS, ECR, ELB and logs", but a user in the Dev account could still create SQS queues and work in us-east-1. Worse, a "deny outside Frankfurt" rule that included route53:* broke DNS completely in the Network account. Route 53 is a global service whose API calls are made through us-east-1, so the request never matched eu-central-1:
An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListHostedZones operation: ... is not authorized to perform: route53:ListHostedZones with an explicit deny in a service control policy - Allow lists are also hard to maintain: every new service your team needs requires an SCP change. We use deny lists.

We will use four custom policies:

  • → Infrastructure, Deployments, Workloads, Sandbox OUs: Rules every member account must follow
  • InfrastructureNetworkManagement → Infrastructure OU: Network account owns connectivity, runs no applications or CI/CD
  • → Deployments OU: Build account owns CI/CD, does not own networking or run applications
  • → Workloads OU: Workload accounts run applications, do not own networking or build images

We don't attach our policies to the Security OU. Control Tower manages the Audit and Log Archive accounts and already protects them with its own guardrails (the aws-guardrails-* policies you can see in the list).

Every Deny statement below has an exception for the AWSControlTowerExecution role and the stacksets-exec-* roles. Control Tower uses these roles to manage the accounts, and blocking them would break enrollment and drift repair.

Policy 1: BaselineGuardrails

Go to AWS Organizations → Policies → Service control policies → Create policy, and name it BaselineGuardrails :

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLeavingOrganization",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "organizations:LeaveOrganization",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyRootUser",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {"ArnLike": {"aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:root"}}
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLongLivedIamCredentials",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["iam:CreateUser", "iam:CreateAccessKey", "iam:CreateLoginProfile"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyDisablingSecurityServices",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "guardduty:DeleteDetector", "guardduty:DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount",
        "guardduty:DisassociateFromMasterAccount", "securityhub:DisableSecurityHub",
        "securityhub:DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount",
        "securityhub:DisassociateFromMasterAccount", "access-analyzer:DeleteAnalyzer"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyOutsideFrankfurt",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "NotAction": [
        "account:*", "acm:*", "aws-marketplace:*", "aws-portal:*", "billing:*", "budgets:*",
        "ce:*", "cloudfront:*", "cur:*", "directconnect:*", "ec2:DescribeRegions",
        "ec2:DescribeTransitGateways", "ec2:DescribeVpnGateways", "ecr-public:*",
        "globalaccelerator:*", "health:*", "iam:*", "kms:*", "networkmanager:*", "organizations:*",
        "pricing:*", "route53:*", "route53domains:*", "s3:GetAccountPublic*",
        "s3:ListAllMyBuckets", "s3:PutAccountPublic*", "shield:*", "sts:*", "support:*",
        "trustedadvisor:*", "waf:*", "wafv2:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": "eu-central-1"},
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
  • DenyLeavingOrganization — an account cannot remove itself from governance.
  • DenyRootUser — the root user of a member account cannot do anything. Everyday access goes through IAM Identity Center.
  • DenyLongLivedIamCredentials — no IAM users, passwords, or access keys. People use Identity Center, and automation uses IAM roles with temporary credentials (for example, GitHub Actions OIDC).
  • DenyDisablingSecurityServices — once GuardDuty, Security Hub, and IAM Access Analyzer are enabled, nobody in a member account can turn them off or detach from the Audit account.
  • DenyOutsideFrankfurt — everything outside eu-central-1 is denied. Note that this uses NotAction: global services such as IAM, STS, Route 53, CloudFront, Organizations, and billing make their API calls through us-east-1, so they must be excluded or they stop working.

Policy 2: InfrastructureNetworkManagement (Infrastructure OU)

The Network account owns connectivity. FullAWSAccess already allows that, so we only add what it must not do: run applications or CI/CD.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyApplicationWorkloads",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "ecs:CreateCluster", "ecs:CreateService", "ecs:RunTask", "eks:CreateCluster",
        "rds:CreateDBInstance", "rds:CreateDBCluster", "apprunner:CreateService",
        "elasticbeanstalk:CreateEnvironment", "lightsail:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyBuildResources",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": ["ecr:CreateRepository", "codebuild:CreateProject", "codepipeline:CreatePipeline"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Policy 3: DeploymentCICDPolicy (Deployments OU)

The Build account owns pipelines and container images. It must not create its own network connectivity (Transit Gateway, peering, VPN, Direct Connect) and must not run application services or databases.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyNetworkConnectivityOwnership",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:CreateTransitGateway", "ec2:CreateVpcPeeringConnection",
        "ec2:AcceptVpcPeeringConnection", "ec2:CreateVpnGateway", "ec2:CreateCustomerGateway",
        "ec2:CreateVpnConnection", "directconnect:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyApplicationRuntime",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "ecs:CreateService", "eks:CreateCluster", "rds:CreateDBInstance", "rds:CreateDBCluster",
        "elasticloadbalancing:CreateLoadBalancer", "apprunner:CreateService",
        "elasticbeanstalk:CreateEnvironment", "lightsail:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Policy 4: WorkloadsECSPolicy (Workloads OU)

Dev and Production run the application. They may attach their VPC to a Transit Gateway shared by the Network account, but cannot build their own connectivity, create ECR repositories, push images, or create pipelines. Images are built once in the Build account and only pulled here.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyNetworkConnectivityOwnership",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "ec2:CreateTransitGateway", "ec2:CreateVpcPeeringConnection",
        "ec2:AcceptVpcPeeringConnection", "ec2:CreateVpnGateway", "ec2:CreateCustomerGateway",
        "ec2:CreateVpnConnection", "directconnect:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyBuildResources",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "ecr:CreateRepository", "ecr:PutImage", "ecr:InitiateLayerUpload",
        "codebuild:CreateProject", "codepipeline:CreatePipeline"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": ["arn:aws:iam::*:role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "arn:aws:iam::*:role/stacksets-exec-*"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Select the policy → Actions → Attach policy, and choose the OU:

  • BaselineGuardrails → Infrastructure, Deployments, Workloads, Sandbox
  • InfrastructureNetworkManagement → Infrastructure
  • DeploymentCICDPolicy → Deployments
  • WorkloadsECSPolicy → Workloads

Leave FullAWSAccess attached. Our policies only take permissions away from it.

The final picture for the Workloads OU should be: FullAWSAccess, the Control Tower aws-guardrails-* policy, BaselineGuardrails, and WorkloadsECSPolicy:

Always test SCPs right after attaching them. EC2 supports --dry-run, which checks permissions without creating anything:

aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --dry-run --profile dev       # UnauthorizedOperation: explicit deny in a service control policy
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --dry-run --profile network   # DryRunOperation: would have succeeded

The error message names the exact SCP that denied the request, which makes troubleshooting much easier. Section 7 has a script that tests all guardrails at once.

before attaching a new SCP to a production OU, attach it to the Sandbox OU or a test account first. A wrong Deny statement affects every account in the OU immediately.

6. Network account: shared VPCs

With the guardrails in place, we can build the network. The Network account owns all VPCs, subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and internet gateways. Dev, Production, and Build don't create VPCs. They receive subnets from the Network account through AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM).

This model is called VPC sharing:

  • The Network account (owner) creates the VPC and controls routing, NAT, and internet access.
  • The workload account (participant) launches its own resources (ECS tasks, load balancers, databases) into the shared subnets and manages its own security groups.
  • The participant cannot modify or delete the VPC, subnets, route tables, or gateways, even with administrator access in its own account.

Why one VPC per environment?

One shared VPC for everyone would put Dev and Production on the same network. Instead, each environment gets its own VPC, shared only with its own account, and we don't need a Transit Gateway yet.

Before creating anything, plan the IP ranges. VPCs that may need to be connected later (with Transit Gateway or peering) must not overlap. Control Tower created a VPC in every account with the same 172.31.0.0/16 range, and these VPCs can never be connected to each other.

We reserve a /16 range for each environment:

Each environment VPC uses two Availability Zones and three subnet tiers:

Load balancers, NAT gateway

The app subnets are larger (/20, about 4,000 addresses) because every ECS task on Fargate gets its own IP address. Production uses the same layout with 10.20.x.x. The build VPC needs only two public and two private subnets (10.30.0.0/24, 10.30.1.0/24, 10.30.16.0/20, 10.30.32.0/20).

Cleaning up the Control Tower VPCs

Control Tower's Account Factory created an empty VPC named aws-controltower-VPC in every new account. We don't need them, so delete them in the Network, Build, Dev, and Production accounts (VPC → Your VPCs → select aws-controltower-VPC → Actions → Delete VPC).

To prevent Control Tower from creating these VPCs in future accounts, go to Control Tower → Account Factory → Network configuration → Edit, and set the maximum number of private subnets to 0.

Sign in to the Network account, open VPC → Create VPC, and choose VPC and more. This wizard creates the VPC, subnets, route tables, internet gateway, NAT gateway, and VPC endpoints in one step.

Use the following settings:

  • Name tag auto-generation: dev
  • IPv4 CIDR block: 10.10.0.0/16, no IPv6
  • Number of Availability Zones: 2 (eu-central-1a and eu-central-1b)
  • Number of public subnets: 2
  • Number of private subnets: 4

Expand Customize subnets CIDR blocks and enter the CIDRs from the table above. The wizard's defaults would give the public subnets /20 ranges, which wastes addresses we want to keep for ECS tasks.

ECS tasks in private subnets need outbound access to pull container images, send logs, and call external APIs. This is the job of the NAT gateway. The wizard offers three options:

  • None — no outbound internet access from private subnets
  • Zonal — a NAT gateway in a specific AZ, either "In 1 AZ" or "1 per AZ"
  • Regional — a single NAT gateway that AWS automatically makes available across your AZs, without managing a NAT gateway and route per AZ

We make a different choice per environment:

  • : Zonal, in 1 AZ. Cheapest. If one AZ fails, dev loses outbound access temporarily, which is acceptable.
  • : Regional. Highly available across AZs without managing one NAT gateway per AZ
  • : Zonal, in 1 AZ. CI/CD can tolerate a short outage

For prod, choose Regional instead of Zonal. There is no AZ selection for a regional NAT gateway, because AWS manages its availability across zones:

Choose S3 Gateway. Gateway endpoints are free. Amazon ECR stores image layers in S3, so most of the traffic when ECS pulls an image goes through the endpoint instead of the NAT gateway, which reduces NAT data processing costs.

We don't create interface endpoints (ECR, CloudWatch Logs, STS) yet. At about $0.01 per hour per AZ each, five of them in two AZs cost more than the NAT gateway they would replace.

Keep DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled.

Before creating the VPC, check the Preview panel on the right. It shows every resource the wizard will create. You should see six subnets, one internet gateway, one NAT gateway, and private route tables with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the NAT gateway.

Click Create VPC. Creating the NAT gateway takes a minute or two.

Open the VPC and look at the Resource map tab. It shows the whole design on one screen: six subnets in two AZs, the public route table pointing to the internet gateway, and the private route tables pointing to the NAT gateway and the S3 endpoint.

Repeat the same steps for prod (10.20.0.0/16, Regional NAT gateway) and build (10.30.0.0/16, 2 public and 2 private subnets, Zonal NAT gateway in 1 AZ).

First, allow RAM to share resources within the organization. In the management account, open Resource Access Manager → Settings and enable Enable sharing with AWS Organizations. Without this setting, resources can only be shared through invitations.

Now, in the Network account, open Resource Access Manager → Resource shares → Create resource share:

  • Resource type: Subnets. Select the six dev subnets
  • Principals: leave "Allow sharing with principals outside your organization" disabled, choose AWS account, and enter the Dev account ID

Create two more shares the same way:

  • prod-network — the six prod subnets, shared with the Production account
  • build-network — only the two build private subnets, shared with the Build account. The Build account doesn't need public subnets, because the SCP denies it from creating load balancers anyway.

Troubleshooting: "can only be shared within your AWS Organization"

When I created the first share, it failed with this error, even though organization sharing was enabled a few minutes earlier:

The message suggests waiting for onboarding to finish, but mine still failed after 40 minutes, from every account. The real hint came from the CLI: sharing with the organization as principal returned UnknownResourceException: Organization o-xxxxxxxx. RAM had never imported the organization, even though the Organizations console listed RAM as a trusted service.

The fix was to reset RAM trusted access from the management account:

aws organizations disable-aws-service-access --service-principal ram.amazonaws.com
aws ram enable-sharing-with-aws-organization

Run this only before you have any resource shares. Disabling trusted access affects existing organization-based shares. After the reset, sharing worked within a minute.

Before that, I ruled out our own SCP by detaching BaselineGuardrails from the Infrastructure OU for a minute. A good habit in a governed account: rule out your own SCPs first. The error message names the denying SCP, as in this example where the region lock blocks CloudTrail in us-east-1:

User: arn:aws:sts::111122223333:assumed-role/AWSReservedSSO_AWSAdministratorAccess_0123456789abcdef/admin
is not authorized to perform: cloudtrail:LookupEvents with an explicit deny in a service control policy:
arn:aws:organizations::444455556666:policy/o-exampleorgid/service_control_policy/p-examplepolicy

Verifying from the Dev account

Sign in to the Dev account and open VPC → Subnets. The shared subnets appear with the Network account as the owner.

Two things may look surprising here:

  • The subnets have no names. Tags are not shared with participant accounts, but you can add your own Name tags in the Dev account.
  • AZ names can differ between accounts: "eu-central-1a" may be a different physical AZ elsewhere. Compare AZ IDs (for example, euc1-az2), not names.
  • The Dev account can now launch ECS services and load balancers into these subnets, but it cannot change routing or create its own internet path.

7. Verify your landing zone

Guardrails are easy to get subtly wrong, so I keep a script that checks the important rules in one run. It only uses read-only calls and EC2 --dry-run, so it never creates anything:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
check() { # name, expected (allow|deny), command...
  local name=$1 expect=$2; shift 2
  out=$("$@" 2>&1); rc=$?
  if echo "$out" | grep -qE 'explicit deny|UnauthorizedOperation|AccessDenied'; then got=deny
  elif echo "$out" | grep -q 'DryRunOperation' || [ $rc -eq 0 ]; then got=allow
  else got="error: $(echo "$out" | tail -1)"; fi
  [ "$got" = "$expect" ] && s=OK || s=FAIL
  printf '%-4s %-48s expected=%-5s got=%s\n' "$s" "$name" "$expect" "$got"
}
check "network: Route 53 works"                 allow aws route53 list-hosted-zones --profile network
check "dev: eu-central-1 allowed"               allow aws ec2 describe-vpcs --profile dev
check "dev: us-east-1 denied (region lock)"     deny  aws ec2 describe-vpcs --region us-east-1 --profile dev
check "dev: IAM (global) still works"           allow aws iam list-roles --max-items 1 --profile dev
check "dev: cannot create Transit Gateway"      deny  aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --dry-run --profile dev
check "build: cannot create Transit Gateway"    deny  aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --dry-run --profile build
check "network: can create Transit Gateway"     allow aws ec2 create-transit-gateway --dry-run --profile network
check "prod: us-west-2 denied (region lock)"    deny  aws ec2 describe-vpcs --region us-west-2 --profile prod

Output from my organization:

OK   network: Route 53 works                          expected=allow got=allow
OK   dev: eu-central-1 allowed                        expected=allow got=allow
OK   dev: us-east-1 denied (region lock)              expected=deny  got=deny
OK   dev: IAM (global) still works                    expected=allow got=allow
OK   dev: cannot create Transit Gateway               expected=deny  got=deny
OK   build: cannot create Transit Gateway             expected=deny  got=deny
OK   network: can create Transit Gateway              expected=allow got=allow
OK   prod: us-west-2 denied (region lock)             expected=deny  got=deny

The "allow" checks matter too: a guardrail that blocks too much is also a bug, like my first region lock that broke Route 53. Run the script after every SCP change.

8. Troubleshooting summary

Every problem I hit while building this part, in one place:

  • Route 53 returns AccessDenied with "explicit deny in a service control policy": A region-lock SCP denied route53:*. Route 53 calls go through us-east-1. Fix: Use NotAction and exclude global services (section 5).
  • An "allow only ECS, ECR, ..." SCP doesn't restrict anything: FullAWSAccess is still attached, and SCPs on the same target are combined. Fix: Keep FullAWSAccess and write Deny statements (section 5).
  • RAM: "can only be shared within your AWS Organization", still failing after 40 minutes: RAM never imported the organization (UnknownResourceException for the org ID). Fix: Disable and re-enable RAM trusted access before creating shares (section 6).
  • Shared subnets have no names in the participant account: Tags aren't shared. Fix: Identify subnets by CIDR or AZ ID, and tag them locally if needed.

If you built this only to learn, delete it in this order. Participants must remove their resources from shared subnets before the owner can delete them.

Dev, Production, and Build accounts: delete anything you launched into the shared subnets, including security groups.

Network account: delete the three RAM shares. Then delete the NAT gateways and release their Elastic IP addresses (this stops most of the cost), and delete the three VPCs.

Management account: detach and delete the four custom SCPs. To remove everything, decommission the landing zone in Control Tower, then close the member accounts. Closed accounts stay suspended for 90 days.

10. Conclusion and what's next

We now have a landing zone where every account has one clear job, and the boundaries are enforced rather than just documented:

  • SCPs make each account's "must not" rules hold, even for administrators. We tested every rule from the CLI.
  • The Network account owns all routing and egress. Each workload account receives only the subnets of its own environment, and it cannot change them.
  • No IAM users and no long-lived keys exist anywhere. All access goes through IAM Identity Center.
  • In part 2, we will set up the Build account on this foundation: CodeCommit without IAM users, an ECR repository that only Dev and Production can pull from, and CodeBuild inside the shared VPC, with its own set of surprises.

items.title: AI Made Us Faster. So Why Do Designers Have Less Time?
items.author: Rinat Seif
items.content:
A poster that used to take me a day now takes a minute to generate. Last night I built an animated website in one evening without writing a single line of code. By every estimate, designers should have half their lives back.

Yet I haven't met a single designer who has more free time. Deadlines are shorter, revisions are longer, and by the evening there are so many options that your eyes start to blur.

So I tried to figure out what is going on. Are we bad at working with AI? Were we sold a fantasy? Or is this just a bubble that is about to pop? The answer turned out to be more interesting than all three.

It feels faster. It turns out slower

In 2025, researchers at METR ran a simple experiment. Sixteen experienced developers worked on real tasks, some with AI tools and some without. Before they started, they expected AI to make them 24% faster.

With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The strangest part: even after the experiment, they believed AI had made them 20% faster.

The study is small, and it is about developers, not designers. But the same picture shows up in much larger surveys:

2,500 workers and executives in 4 countries

96% of executives expect AI to raise productivity. 77% of employees say it added to their workload

52 interviews, 300+ public AI initiatives

95% of organizations got zero return from generative AI

Computers went through the same thing in the 1980s. Economist Robert Solow famously observed that you could see the computer age everywhere except in the productivity statistics. The growth did come, but only after people rebuilt the way they worked.

Where the saved time goes

I see three reasons, and none of them is that the models are bad.

1. Generation got cheap. Choosing didn't. A designer used to make three options and bring the best one. Now you can get 200 in an hour. Each one has to be looked at, compared, and rejected for a reason. Nobody counts that time, but it eats all the savings.

2. Clients know generation takes a minute too. So "by Friday" turned into "by tomorrow", and one round of revisions turned into five. Economists call this the Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper, we consume more of it. Cheap images didn't reduce the work. They increased the appetite.

3. We dropped AI into the old process. Brief, references, sketches, approvals all stayed the same. There is just a new "generate" button in the middle. According to Upwork, 47% of employees using AI don't know how to reach the productivity gains their managers expect. And in the MIT report, the 5% of companies that succeeded rebuilt the process itself instead of buying one more tool.

There is one more thing METR showed. With AI, the feeling of speed and actual speed drift apart. Generating gives you the sense that work is happening even when it is stuck. For designers, it looks like an hour of rerolling one frame instead of five minutes thinking about what exactly is wrong with it.

Fair question. In June 2026, JPMorgan estimated global AI infrastructure spending at $5.5 trillion through 2030. The largest cloud providers alone are spending about $650 billion in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money. Investors argue about one thing: whether demand will catch up with the spending.

For designers, I think something else matters more. Even if the financial bubble pops, the tools won't disappear. After the dot-com crash in 2000, the internet didn't go away. The companies that couldn't make money on it did, and the ones that could grew in their place.

AI looks similar. If there is a bubble, it is in expectations: "buy a subscription and everything gets faster." The data above shows it doesn't work that way. But the change in the profession has already happened, and it won't roll back.

More designers, less foundation

There is another tension in the industry. Open Threads and it looks like everyone is a designer now. The profession has ballooned and is changing in front of us. But behind a lot of those generations is a lack of basics: composition, grids, typography. AI doesn't fix that. It mass-produces it.

That is especially true for product designers moving from interfaces into visual work. A component library keeps a UI consistent, but there is no Storybook for light, texture and framing.

What I do to make the speed real

  1. I decide before the first generation, and I set a limit. Light, background, palette and grid are written down in advance. Only the object changes in the prompt. If three rerolls don't get the frame right, I stop and put into words what exactly is wrong.
  2.  Every frame of the series on one screen, then I remove the one that doesn't fit. Comparing them one by one in a chat window takes many times longer.
  3.  Three directions with a rationale, not a folder of 50 images. The more options a client sees, the longer they take to decide and the more revisions they send.

None of these steps requires a new model. They are all about who is running the process.

We weren't fooled. We were sold faster execution and assumed we had bought faster work. AI speeds up making things. It doesn't free up a designer's time on its own. The person who frees up time is the one who decided in advance what they are making and knows how to choose quickly.

That animated website from the first paragraph took one evening for exactly that reason: I knew what feeling I wanted before I typed the first prompt. Without that, I would still be rerolling it.

Has AI saved you time, or eaten it? And how have your deadlines changed in the last year?

items.title: Six Password Reset Vulnerabilities and How to Prevent Them
items.author: HackerMe
items.content:
This is an example, not a report from a customer. Imagine a support inbox: someone never asked for a password reset, but they received a "your password was changed" email, and now their login no longer works. Their old password was long and unique. Nobody guessed it.

Nobody needed to. A reset flow is a way into an account without the current password, by design. A valid reset link may let whoever holds it set a new password. Whether that is enough to take the account depends on other controls: a second factor at the reset step, a prompt to re-authenticate, a notification the real owner sees in time, session invalidation after the change, or a token that has already expired or been used.

OWASP calls this functionality "a common source of vulnerabilities" even though it "looks straightforward and easy to implement" (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet). The usual weak points sit at six places in the flow. Run the active tests only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

1. The request should say the same thing to everyone

When someone types an address into "Forgot password", the response should not reveal whether an account exists. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet lists "We just sent you a password reset link" and "This email address doesn't exist in our database" as incorrect responses, and gives the correct one: "If that email address is in our database, we will send you an email to reset your password" (OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet).

The message is the easy part. The Forgot Password Cheat Sheet also asks for responses that "return in a consistent amount of time," for example by sending the email asynchronously instead of exiting early for unknown addresses. A page that answers in a few milliseconds for unknown addresses and noticeably later for real ones tells an attacker the same thing as a different message.

Then rate-limit the endpoint. OWASP recommends per-account rate limiting or a CAPTCHA, because otherwise an attacker can flood a user's inbox. Return the same whether or not the account exists (RFC 6585, section 4), or the limiter itself becomes an enumeration oracle. Do not lock the account: OWASP notes that a forgotten-password attack should not produce a lockout, because that lets anyone deny access to users whose names they know.

2. Build the link from configuration, never from the request

Many frameworks make it easy to build an absolute URL from "the current host". In a reset email, that convenience is the vulnerability. PortSwigger describes password reset poisoning: an attacker submits a reset request for the victim with a Host header pointing at a domain they control, the site sends a genuine token, and the link inside points at the attacker. If the victim clicks it, or a mail scanner fetches it, the token is delivered to the attacker (PortSwigger: Password reset poisoning).

OWASP's instruction is direct: "Don't rely on the Host header while creating the reset URLs." Use one configured HTTPS base URL per environment, and reject host names you do not serve. Treat the same way: trust it only from your own proxy.

3. The token: random, long, hashed, single-use, short-lived

OWASP lists the properties every reset token needs: generated with a cryptographically secure random number generator, long enough to resist brute force, linked to an individual user, invalidated after use, stored securely, and expiring after an appropriate period.

Here is a minimal sketch in Python that follows those properties. It is something to adapt, not a drop-in library.

import hashlib, secrets, time

TOKEN_TTL = 30 * 60
BASE_URL = "https://shop.example"  # from configuration, never from the request
_store = {}  # token_hash -> {"user_id", "expires", "used"}; use your database

def _hash(token):
    return hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()

def issue_reset_link(user_id, now=None):
    now = time.time() if now is None else now
    for rec in _store.values():
        if rec["user_id"] == user_id:
            rec["used"] = True
    token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    _store[_hash(token)] = {"user_id": user_id, "expires": now + TOKEN_TTL, "used": False}
    return f"{BASE_URL}/reset?token={token}"

def redeem(token, now=None):
    now = time.time() if now is None else now
    if not isinstance(token, str) or not token:
        return None
    rec = _store.get(_hash(token))
    if rec is None or rec["used"] or now > rec["expires"]:
        return None
    rec["used"] = True
    return rec["user_id"]

secrets.token_urlsafe(32) uses Python's module for security tokens, which documents 32 bytes (256 bits) of randomness as sufficient for the typical case (Python docs: secrets). Never use , timestamps, user IDs or sequential values. Store only a hash, so a leaked database does not contain working links. For a long random token, a fast hash such as SHA-256 is a reasonable choice; slow password hashing is meant for secrets people choose (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet). Issuing a new token should burn older ones for that user. An expired, used or unknown token should produce the same generic error page.

The sketch is single-process and in-memory. In a real application, two requests can redeem the same token at once, so marking it used must be one atomic database operation that succeeds only if it changes exactly one unused, unexpired row.

4. Keep the token where you put it

The token sits in a URL, and URLs travel.

OWASP asks reset pages to send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. When no policy is set, browsers default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, which sends only the origin on cross-origin requests (MDN: Referrer-Policy). A missing header is not proof that the token leaks to third parties in current browsers. It is a missing layer: the default still sends the full URL on same-origin requests, and a looser policy elsewhere on the site would apply.

Analytics, chat widgets and session-replay tools on the reset page can read . The cleanest pattern is a reset page with no third-party scripts. Mail scanners can also open the link before the user does. If a GET burns the single-use token, the real user may find it "already used". Show the form on GET, and consume the token only on POST.

5. After the reset, end the old sessions

If an attacker already had a session, a new password alone does not remove them. OWASP recommends invalidating existing sessions, or asking the user whether to do so, and advises against signing the user in automatically after the reset. The Session Management Cheat Sheet lists a completed password change among the events that should require reauthentication (OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet).

Send a notification that the password was changed, without the password in it, as OWASP recommends. In the example above, that email is what turned a silent change into a support ticket. Include a way to report "this wasn't me" that does not depend on the account's current password.

How to test your own flow

Use two test accounts you control, and staging where possible. We have not run the commands below against a live site.

Submit the form for a real test address and for an address that does not exist, and compare status, visible message, size and timing. You want the same status and message for both. A "no such user" error is a leak. Small size differences can come from a CSRF token; timing needs many requests before it means anything.

In staging, send the same request with a foreign (and again with ) and read the email that arrives. If the link points at the foreign host, that header is being trusted. A or from the proxy only shows that this request was refused; read the link-building code as well.

With a test account, reuse a spent link, use the older of two links, wait past expiry, and open the page with GET before submitting the form. The last check shows whether a GET burns the token. Look at the reset page for and third-party scripts. After a reset, a second browser that was already signed in should be signed out or asked to authenticate again.

If every step behaved as intended for these test accounts, this flow did what you asked when you tested it. Other recovery paths, and the difference between staging and production, still need their own review.

We are the HackerMe team, and we build a free scanner for public pages and headers. It cannot read reset emails or token storage.

items.title: Benchmarking AWS Amplify, Lambda, Web Functions, and ECS for Next.js
items.author: Tokarev Artem
items.content:
"Should this run on Amplify, Lambda or ECS?" is usually answered with a feature list. I wanted numbers. So I took one Next.js app, deployed it to four AWS runtimes in the same account and Region, including the new Lambda Web Functions, and measured the things that decide the choice in practice: latency under load, cold starts, CPU speed, real limits, and the monthly bill at four traffic levels.

Lambda and ECS run the exact same container image, and the Web Function runs the same files from a .zip. Amplify Hosting builds the same Git commit. Every command, script, and result is in a public repository, with deploy and cleanup steps:

Four results surprised me:

  • One ECS Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU was the fastest option for light requests, then failed completely under load: at 200 requests per second, 29% of page requests returned errors, and ECS replaced the overloaded task twice during my tests.
  • Lambda, Lambda Web Functions and Amplify kept the same latency from 10 to 200 requests per second with zero errors.
  • The new Web Functions had the fastest CPU and no 6 MB response limit, but in my test they cost about four times as much as classic Lambda, because idle environments are billed for memory.
  • Amplify cuts every request at about 28 seconds and every response at 6 MB, and classic Lambda behind a Function URL also stops at 6 MB.

One app, four runtimes, one DynamoDB table:

  • builds the app from GitHub and runs the server-side code on its own managed compute.
  • (a classic function, which AWS now calls an Event Function) runs the container image through the Lambda Web Adapter, exposed with a Function URL. Each execution environment handles one request at a time.
  • run the same Next.js server from a .zip as a real HTTP server, with no adapter. Each environment handles many requests at once, and you pay for active CPU time instead of wall-clock time.
  • runs the same image as a service behind an Application Load Balancer.

The app has a few endpoints, each testing something different:

  • : a server-rendered page that reads one DynamoDB item, the typical "real page"
  • : no I/O at all, to measure the runtime's own overhead
  • : one DynamoDB GetItem, a typical API call
  • : 50,000 chained SHA-256 hashes, to compare the CPU you actually get
  • and : to find the real request timeout and response size limit

Every response reports which runtime served it, the CPU architecture, and whether it was the first request of that process (a cold start):

{"runtime":"lambda","cold":true,"requestsServed":1,"arch":"arm64","node":"v22.23.5","memoryMb":1024}

2. Prerequisites and cost

  • An AWS account and the AWS CLI v2 with credentials for it. Web Functions need a recent version with the commands (I used 2.40.4); run to check.
  • Docker with buildx, Node.js 22, and k6 for the load tests
  • A GitHub account for Amplify Hosting

Everything runs in eu-central-1. Lambda and Fargate use arm64 (Graviton) and roughly the same size: Lambda with 1024 MB of memory, and a Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. A Web Function environment has a fixed size of 2 arm64 vCPUs and 2 GB, which you can't change, and Amplify chooses its own compute.

While the setup is running, the only fixed cost is the ECS part: the load balancer, one Fargate task and four public IPv4 addresses, about $1.90 per day. Lambda, Amplify and DynamoDB cost close to nothing at test traffic. Run the cleanup script when you are done.

3. The app and one image for two runtimes

The app is a normal Next.js app router project. The only special setting is the standalone output, which produces a small self-contained for the container. Amplify builds the app its own way, so the setting is applied only in the Docker build:

const config: NextConfig = {
  output: process.env.STANDALONE ? "standalone" : undefined,
  poweredByHeader: false,
};

The Dockerfile is where Lambda and ECS meet:

FROM node:22-alpine
COPY --from=public.ecr.aws/awsguru/aws-lambda-adapter:0.9.1 /lambda-adapter /opt/extensions/lambda-adapter
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 \
    AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PATH=/api/health
COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static
RUN rm -rf .next/cache && ln -s /tmp/next-cache .next/cache
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
  • The is copied into . Lambda starts everything in that folder as an extension, and the adapter turns each invoke event into a normal HTTP request to . On ECS, nothing starts it, so the same image is a plain web server.
  • The points to a separate route. My first version used , and the adapter's readiness probe became the "first request" of every process, so no request ever looked cold. Health checks should not touch the code you measure.
  • The is moved to , because Lambda's file system is read-only everywhere else.

Build for arm64 and push to ECR:

aws ecr create-repository --repository-name runtime-benchmark \
  --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --provenance=false \
  -t "$REPO_URI:$IMAGE_TAG" --push .

keeps a plain single-platform image. By default, buildx adds an attestation manifest and pushes an image index, which Lambda may refuse to use. The script tags each image with the Git commit, so an immutable tag always matches one commit.

Scan on push found one critical CVE on the first push, in from the base image, not in the app. Base images are rebuilt on a schedule, so security fixes can be days old before they reach the tag you pull. One line in the final stage fixed it:

RUN apk upgrade --no-cache

The next image scanned with zero findings. The compressed image is 88 MB in ECR (233 MB unpacked).

The DynamoDB table is on-demand with one item. Each runtime gets its own IAM role with exactly one permission, on this table.

4. Lambda with a Function URL

aws lambda create-function --function-name runtime-benchmark --package-type Image \
  --code ImageUri="$REPO_URI:$IMAGE_TAG" --architectures arm64 \
  --role "$ROLE_ARN" --memory-size 1024 --timeout 30 \
  --environment "Variables={RUNTIME_NAME=lambda,TABLE_NAME=runtime-benchmark,APP_REGION=eu-central-1}"

aws lambda create-function-url-config --function-name runtime-benchmark --auth-type NONE
aws lambda add-permission --function-name runtime-benchmark --statement-id public-url \
  --action lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl --principal '*' --function-url-auth-type NONE
aws lambda add-permission --function-name runtime-benchmark --statement-id public-invoke \
  --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal '*' --invoked-via-function-url

A public Function URL now needs both permissions: , and limited to calls that come through the URL. I removed the second one to check, and the URL answered with 403 and a helpful message:

{"Message":"Forbidden. Invoking a Function URL requires both the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions."}

A Function URL is free and needs no API Gateway. For production, you would usually put CloudFront in front of it for a custom domain, caching and AWS WAF.

The quota that new accounts don't tell you about

Before load testing, check this:

aws lambda get-account-settings --query 'AccountLimit.ConcurrentExecutions'
10

The documented default is 1,000 concurrent executions, but my account had 10. Ten concurrent requests at about 100 ms each is roughly 100 requests per second, and anything above returns . I requested an increase in Service Quotas (quota code L-B99A9384).

The increase to 1,000 was approved automatically after 2 hours and 20 minutes. Lambda's fast endpoints need far less concurrency than you might expect: at about 40 ms per request, 50 requests per second keep only 2 to 3 environments busy. The CPU endpoint at 50 requests per second peaked at 57 concurrent executions, well over the original limit.

Lambda Web Functions are a new kind of Lambda function for HTTP traffic. Your code is a normal web server that listens on a port, Lambda gives it an HTTPS endpoint, and each execution environment serves many requests at the same time, like a container. It still scales to zero when there is no traffic.

  • Node.js only (), deployed as a .zip from a versioned S3 bucket. No container images.
  • Arm64 only. Each environment has 2 vCPUs and 2 GB of memory, and you can't change that.
  • Your server must listen on the address in () within 10 seconds of startup.
  • Each environment handles up to 64 concurrent requests by default (maxConcurrencyPerEnvironment, 1 to 128), and Lambda lowers that limit dynamically based on resource usage.

The Next.js standalone server reads and instead, so the entry file maps one to the other:

// index.js: the Web Function entry file
const [host, port] = (process.env.AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT || "localhost:3000").split(":");
process.env.HOSTNAME = host;
process.env.PORT = port;
require("./server.js");

To keep the comparison fair, I didn't rebuild the app. The deploy script copies out of the same linux/arm64 container image, adds , and deploys that folder:

cid=$(docker create --platform linux/arm64 "$REPO_URI:$IMAGE_TAG")
docker cp "$cid:/app/." build/web-function/ && docker rm "$cid"
cp web-function/index.js build/web-function/

aws lambda-web deploy --name runtime-benchmark-web --code build/web-function \
  --create --include-hidden-files \
  --execution-role-arn "$ROLE_ARN" \
  --env RUNTIME_NAME=lambda-web --env TABLE_NAME=runtime-benchmark --env APP_REGION=eu-central-1 \
  --timeout-seconds 30 --endpoint-name main --auth-type ApplicationManaged

is easy to miss: the Next.js build lives in , and without the flag the command leaves hidden folders out of the package. creates the S3 bucket, the function, the first revision and a public endpoint, and waits until the endpoint is active. My first deploy took under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of code and configuration. Changing an environment variable means a new revision, and an endpoint can route traffic to one revision or split it between two, which gives you canary deployments without CodeDeploy.

The pricing model is different from classic Lambda. In eu-central-1 you pay $0.30 per million requests, $0.000035 per vCPU-second of CPU time that your code actually uses, and $0.0000046 per GB-second of memory for the whole life of each environment. A request that waits for DynamoDB uses almost no CPU, so it costs very little. But an environment that stays alive costs memory time even between requests: one environment kept alive for a month is about $24 in memory alone.

6. ECS Fargate behind a load balancer, without a NAT gateway

A Fargate task in a private subnet needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints to pull its image, and either costs more than the task itself. For this test, the tasks run in public subnets with a public IP, and the security groups do the protecting:

  • The ALB security group allows port 80 from the internet
  • the task security group allows port 3000 only from the ALB security group
aws ecs register-task-definition --family runtime-benchmark \
  --requires-compatibilities FARGATE --network-mode awsvpc --cpu 512 --memory 1024 \
  --runtime-platform cpuArchitecture=ARM64,operatingSystemFamily=LINUX \
  --execution-role-arn "$EXEC_ROLE_ARN" --task-role-arn "$TASK_ROLE_ARN" \
  --container-definitions file://container.json

aws ecs create-service --cluster runtime-benchmark --service-name runtime-benchmark \
  --task-definition runtime-benchmark --desired-count 1 --launch-type FARGATE \
  --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[$SUBNETS],securityGroups=[$TASK_SG],assignPublicIp=ENABLED}" \
  --load-balancers targetGroupArn="$TG_ARN",containerName=app,containerPort=3000

Two roles, two jobs: the execution role lets ECS pull the image and write logs, and the task role is what your code runs as. The DynamoDB permission goes on the task role only.

Two settings save time on every deploy. The target group health check uses every 10 seconds with a healthy threshold of 2, so a new task gets traffic in about 20 seconds. The deregistration delay is 10 seconds instead of the default 300, so an old task stops quickly.

One bug from my script is worth sharing: separates a list of subnet IDs with tabs, not spaces. My script turned spaces into commas, so the service request got one "subnet ID" with tabs inside and failed with Subnet ID must match subnet-[0-9a-f]+. Pipe the list through .

Amplify Hosting connects to GitHub with its own GitHub App. It does not use an AWS CodeConnections connection, even if you already have one for CodeBuild or CodePipeline. So the first step is in the console: Create new app, GitHub, choose the repository and the main branch. Amplify detects Next.js and uses the from the repository.

Environment variables don't reach your server code

This is the biggest surprise for anyone coming from Lambda or ECS. Amplify passes environment variables to the build, not to the server-side code at runtime. The fix is to write the variables your server code needs into during the build:

build:
  commands:
    - env | grep -E '^(RUNTIME_NAME|TABLE_NAME|APP_REGION)=' >> .env.production || true
    - npm run build

The is there because my first build failed without it. Before the variables were set, found nothing and exited with code 1, and Amplify stopped the build with "Command failed with exit code 1".

Two more rules: variable names can't start with , so the app reads instead of , and secrets should not go into this way, because they end up in the build artifact.

The server-side code needs AWS credentials to call DynamoDB. Amplify calls this a compute role: an IAM role that can assume.

aws iam create-role --role-name runtime-benchmark-amplify-compute \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://amplify-trust.json
aws amplify update-app --app-id "$APP_ID" --platform WEB_COMPUTE \
  --compute-role-arn "$COMPUTE_ROLE_ARN" \
  --environment-variables RUNTIME_NAME=amplify,TABLE_NAME=runtime-benchmark,APP_REGION=eu-central-1

Without a compute role, the page renders but the DynamoDB call fails with a credentials error.

The first response from Amplify answered a question the console doesn't:

{"runtime":"amplify","cold":true,"arch":"x64","memoryMb":1024}

AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE is set, so the server code runs on Lambda with 1024 MB, on x64, managed by Amplify. You can't choose the memory size or arm64, and it doesn't count against your account's Lambda concurrency quota.

  • k6 on a laptop in London, against the default URL of each runtime. Absolute latencies include my network path; the differences between runtimes are what matter.
  • a constant arrival rate (k6 ) of 10, 50 and 200 requests per second for 2 minutes per endpoint, with p50, p95 and p99.
  • for Lambda, the script changes an environment variable before each request, which retires all warm environments, and repeats this 10 times. For Amplify, it sends one request after 20 minutes of no traffic. ECS has no cold starts while a task runs.
  • and with increasing values.
k6 run -e BASE_URL=$URL -e ENDPOINT=/api/item -e RATE=50 -e DURATION=2m bench/load.js
bench/coldstart.sh lambda 10
bench/limits.sh lambda $URL

At 10 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 1,200 requests each):

On light requests, ECS is the fastest, Lambda and the Web Function are close behind with almost the same medians, and Amplify is about 1.5 times slower than Lambda. ECS wins here because nothing sits between the load balancer and a warm Node.js process.

The CPU row is the surprise. One Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU could not keep up with 10 CPU-heavy requests per second: each request needs about 80 to 150 ms of CPU, so the work arrived faster than half a vCPU could do it. Requests queued, the ALB health checks timed out, and ECS replaced the "unhealthy" task in the middle of the test. 8% of requests failed and the median rose to 1.9 seconds. Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify handled the same load without errors, because they add execution environments as the load grows.

The lesson is not that ECS is slow. A fixed-size service needs auto scaling and headroom, and a health check that shares the CPU with the work it checks can turn an overload into a restart.

At 200 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 24,000 requests each):

Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify barely noticed the twentyfold increase: their medians moved by a few milliseconds and no request failed. For the Web Function, I ran the 200 requests per second test twice, because AWS says the first load test on a new Web Function scales conservatively, and the table shows the second run. The two runs were within a few milliseconds of each other. Lambda scaled to 234 concurrent executions in the first seconds of the test, then settled between 50 and 90, with zero throttles.

The single ECS task reached 100% CPU and failed. At 50 requests per second the same task used about 65% CPU on the page endpoint, so one 0.5 vCPU task handles roughly 70 page requests per second before it falls over. For real traffic, you would run at least two tasks with target tracking auto scaling at 50 to 60% CPU.

The 50 requests per second results look like the 10 requests per second ones for Lambda, ECS and Amplify, so I left them in the repository instead of adding another table.

One more number explains why Lambda looks so fast: its billed duration (the CloudWatch Duration metric) was 9 to 16 ms at the median for the light endpoints. Most of the 40 ms that the client sees is the network and the Function URL, not your code.

The CPU endpoint does the same 50,000 hashes everywhere:

  • about 150 ms billed duration per request, 155 to 182 ms at the client
  • Web Function, 2 vCPUs, arm64: 96 to 102 ms at the median at the client, the fastest of the four
  • 204 to 217 ms at the client
  • Fargate, 0.5 vCPU, arm64: 79 ms for a single request on an idle task, but it cannot sustain that: at 10 requests per second the task collapsed

Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory: one full vCPU at 1,769 MB. At 1024 MB you get a bit more than half a vCPU, and you pay for the milliseconds you use. A Web Function environment always has 2 vCPUs, and you pay only for the CPU time you use. Node.js runs JavaScript on one thread, so a single request can use only one of them, but that one is a full vCPU. Fargate gives you exactly the vCPU you reserve, all the time, whether you use it or not.

Lambda, 10 forced cold starts (the script changes an environment variable before each request):

  • Init Duration in the Lambda logs: 768 to 941 ms, about 820 ms at the median
  • First request at the client: 1.04 to 1.36 s, about 1.1 s at the median
  • The next request on the same environment: 100 to 195 ms
  • The very first cold start after deploying a new image took 3.7 s of init and 4.2 s at the client, because Lambda had not cached the new image yet

Amplify, one request after 20 minutes without traffic, 3 times: 1.94 s, 2.00 s and 0.33 s, compared with about 0.16 s for a warm request. All three were served by a new process, so the third one probably landed on an environment that Amplify had already prepared. You can't see or control this, so plan for about 2 seconds on the first request after a quiet period.

Web Function, 5 forced cold starts (each run creates a new revision, which starts new environments):

  • First request at the client: 0.95 to 1.21 s, about 1.02 s at the median
  • The next request on the same environment: 140 to 300 ms
  • After the 200 requests per second test ended, the environments stayed alive for about 5 minutes before Lambda removed them. One environment that I woke up with 7 requests stayed alive for more than 6 minutes. A site that gets a request every few minutes will rarely see a Web Function cold start, and that matters for the cost below.

ECS has no cold start while a task is running, which is what you pay the fixed monthly price for. Scaling out is a different story: in the ECS events, a replacement task registered with the load balancer about 25 seconds after it started, and then needed two 10-second health checks before it got traffic. A new Lambda environment was ready in about one second.

I asked each runtime to wait longer and longer, and to return larger and larger responses:

  • Lambda stopped at 30 seconds with 502, which is the function timeout I configured; you can raise it to 15 minutes. The Web Function stopped at 30 seconds with 504 and the header lambda-web-error-type: Runtime.RequestTimeout; its also goes up to 15 minutes. ECS stopped at 60 seconds with 504, the ALB idle timeout, which you can raise to 4,000 seconds. Amplify stopped every request at about 28 seconds with 504, and you can't change that.
  • Lambda returned 5 MB but failed at 6 MB with 502, the payload limit for buffered responses. Amplify also returned 5 MB and failed at 6 MB, with 413. ECS returned 20 MB without trouble, because nothing between the ALB and the container limits the size. The Web Function also returned 20 MB, because it streams responses by default.

If your app has report downloads, file exports or slow third-party calls, these limits decide more than any latency number. Classic Lambda can go beyond 6 MB with response streaming, but that needs code changes. With Web Functions, you get it without changes.

10. What it costs per month

Prices are on-demand prices in eu-central-1 from the AWS Price List API, in November 2026, without free tiers:

  • $0.20 per million requests plus $0.0000133 per GB-second. The Function URL is free.
  • Lambda Web Functions (arm64): $0.30 per million requests, $0.000035 per vCPU-second of CPU time actually used, and $0.0000046 per GB-second of memory for the whole life of each environment. Each environment has 2 GB, so one environment that stays alive all month costs $24.35 in memory.
  • $0.30 per million requests plus $0.20 per GB-hour, which is about $0.0000556 per GB-second, 4.2 times the Lambda arm64 rate. Data out is $0.15 per GB, and builds are $0.01 per minute.
  • Fargate arm64 at $0.03725 per vCPU-hour and $0.00409 per GB-hour, so one 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB task is $16.58 per month. The ALB is $0.027 per hour ($19.71 per month) plus LCUs. Public IPv4 addresses are $0.005 per hour each: the ALB has one per Availability Zone and each task has one, so four addresses add $14.60 per month.

What my Web Function test actually cost

Web Functions publish their own usage in CloudWatch (, and in the namespace), so I could calculate the real bill for my load tests instead of estimating it:

  • 147,608 requests in about 20 minutes
  • 3,966 vCPU-seconds of CPU, which is 27 ms per request on average
  • 48,354 environment-seconds (13.4 environment-hours) at 2 GB each
  • Cost: $0.04 for requests, $0.14 for CPU, $0.45 for memory, $0.63 in total, or $4.28 per million requests

71% of the bill was memory. At 200 requests per second, Lambda ran up to 55 environments, and none of them served more than 2 requests at the same time (the EnvironmentConcurrentRequests maximum). That was the case in both 200 requests per second runs. AWS documents that a new Web Function starts with a conservative per-environment concurrency limit and raises it as it learns, but I didn't see that happen in about 25 minutes of testing. About 30% of the memory time came after the test, while the environments waited about 5 minutes before Lambda removed them.

The same request mix on classic Lambda would cost about $0.15, or $1.04 per million requests. So in my test, Web Functions cost about four times as much. If the per-environment concurrency grows over time, as AWS describes, this gap will shrink, so treat it as the cost of a new function under a load test, not a final verdict.

Monthly cost at four traffic levels

For the monthly bill, I used the measured durations: 20 ms of Lambda billed time per request (the 9 to 16 ms median, rounded up), and 5 KB per response. Amplify doesn't publish its billed compute time per request; its CloudWatch Latency metric averaged about 100 ms, which includes the CDN, so I show 100 ms as the upper bound and 30 ms as a likely lower bound. ECS uses the measured capacity of about 50 requests per second per task with headroom. For the Web Function, I used 27 ms of CPU per request, at least one environment alive all month (requests arrive more often than every 5 minutes at these levels), and the measured 0.24 environments per request per second at steady load.

  • ECS has a floor of about $57 per month before the first request: $16.58 for the task, $19.71 for the ALB, about $6 for LCUs and $14.60 for four public IPv4 addresses. A second task for availability adds about $20.
  • Web Functions have a soft floor of about $24 per month, one 2 GB environment kept alive by regular traffic. With traffic that stops for long periods, the environment scales to zero and the floor disappears. Above that floor, the CPU-based billing is cheap: 10 million requests add only about $12.
  • Lambda stays cheapest until about 100 million requests per month for this light app. 100 million requests is 38 requests per second on average, so a real service would hit that level only with steady traffic.
  • Heavy requests make both more expensive. At 150 ms per request (the CPU endpoint), Lambda costs about 7.5 times more than at 20 ms. But one 0.5 vCPU task sustains only about 3 such requests per second, so ECS needs many more tasks too. Per request they end up close, and Lambda still has no monthly floor.

The script is in the repository (), so you can run it with your own durations and response sizes.
