DORA describes AI adoption as a J-curve: teams often see a temporary dip while they learn the tools and adjust workflows, before longer-term returns show up. Escalation work is a good place to look early because the effort is easy to count. At Higher Logic, support shipped fixes for 50 customer issues within two months of its PlayerZero pilot.

How is this different from DORA's AI ROI framework?

DORA's framework models the financial return of AI-assisted development across software delivery as a whole. PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator focuses on one place that return leaks: the effort escalated customer issues pull from support, engineering, product, and QA. Used together, they show both the overall picture and a specific, recoverable source of capacity.

items.title: Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16-GGUF: Everything Developers Need to Know
items.author: aimodels44
items.content:
A GGUF conversion of Tencent’s Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 draft model, intended for speculative decoding with a separate Qwen3.8-27B target model in a llama.cpp fork. It is not a standalone chat model. The maintainer is aj9o9.

Use it to accelerate Qwen3.8-27B generation, especially code, math, and tool-call workloads. The supplied RTX 3090 tests also show gains on mixed chat tasks, but prose and image-heavy requests may benefit less; tune draft length for your GPU and workload.

Requires both a compatible Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF and the branch of the llama.cpp fork; stock llama.cpp does not load these files. Longer drafts consume more VRAM and reduce available context: on the tested 24 GB RTX 3090 setup, Q4_K_M with 15 drafted tokens fit up to context 65,536, versus 98,304 with 7 drafted tokens. Speculative decoding can produce different output from non-speculative runs, including at temperature 0. Performance figures are hardware-, backend-, prompt-, and setting-dependent; community results use differing test conditions.

On the tested RTX 3090, Q4_K_M DSpine at 15 drafted tokens reached 90.1 tok/s on a mixed short-context task set, compared with 51.7 tok/s for DFlash2 and 28.2 tok/s without speculation. Code and math were the strongest measured tasks; prose was slower than code and math. The same test setup reported maximum context of 65,536 for DSpine at 15 drafts, 98,304 for DFlash2 at 7 drafts, and 176,128 without speculation. These are results for the stated setup, not general rankings. Other GGUF alternatives listed in the supplied sources include Qwen3.8-27B-S-mirai-GGUF, Qwen-3.8-27B-ROCmFP4-FAST-GGUF, Qwen3.8-27B-i1-IQ4_KS_KT-GGUF, and Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF.

This is a five-layer speculative drafter that reads hidden states from five target-model layers and drafts a 16-token block in parallel. Its described mechanisms include causal block attention, a gated code bridge after each layer, and serial last-write refinement over candidate predecessor tokens. Available files are Q4_K_M (1.26 GB; code-bridge tensors remain BF16), Q8_0 (2.20 GB), and BF16 (4.06 GB, described as intended for re-quantizing). The files contain only the drafter. The supplied RTX 3090 benchmark used a Q4_K_M Qwen3.8-27B target, q8_0 KV caches, one slot, and the CUDA branch. It measured 90.1 tok/s on a mixed task set at temperature 0; task-specific results were 128.7 tok/s for code, 122.8 for math, 62.0 for summarize/translate, and 41.6 for prose/story. These are reported measurements, not guarantees. The supplied abstract describes DSpine research results on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in SGLang; it does not establish those results as measurements of this GGUF conversion or its Qwen3.8-27B use.

Use a compatible Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF together with one of the drafter GGUF files. The documented llama.cpp server setup accepts a target path () and drafter path (), with controls including , context size (), slot count (), and optional probabilistic draft sampling. The README warns that auto-fit may not reserve enough memory for the drafter; set context size explicitly. On 24 GB cards, two slots with 15-token drafts do not fit according to the supplied guidance.

The drafter proposes token blocks for speculative verification by the target model; it does not independently provide final text generation. The decoder can select a draft chain greedily or by sampling. Output may differ from a run without a drafter because verification batches tokens and can change near-tied token choices; the source says code and tool calls usually match, while prose and image descriptions can diverge.

git clone -b dspine https://github.com/Ajay9o9/llama.cpp.git
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON
cmake --build build --config Release -j

./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -md Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-dflash \
  --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  -ngl 999 --spec-draft-ngl 999 \
  -fa on --jinja -c 32768 -np 1 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0

The example is the documented CUDA setup. Adjust and for your GPU and memory; the source recommends testing draft sizes such as 2, 3, 4, 7, and 15.

Frequently asked questions

Q: Can I use this as a standalone model?

A: No. These files contain only the draft model; pair one with a Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF.

Q: Will stock llama.cpp load the files?

A: No. The supplied README says they require the branch of the Ajay9o9 llama.cpp fork; stock llama.cpp refuses to load them.

Q: Which quantization should I start with?

A: The README recommends Q4_K_M, whose code-bridge tensors remain BF16. Q8_0 is larger and uses more VRAM, while BF16 is described as a full-precision file for re-quantizing.

Q: What draft length should I set?

A: The documented default of 3 uses only part of the 16-token block. The source suggests trying 2, 3, 4, 7, and 15; 15 is a starting point for CUDA, ROCm/HIP, and SYCL, while AMD Vulkan may favor 2 or 3.

Q: How much context fits on a 24 GB GPU?

A: In the reported RTX 3090 setup with a Q4_K_M target and q8_0 KV cache, the maximum context was 65,536 with 15 drafted tokens and 98,304 with 7. Actual capacity depends on the setup.

Q: Does speculative decoding preserve identical output?

A: Not necessarily, even at temperature 0. Batched verification can change near-tied token choices; the source reports that code and tool calls usually match, while prose and image descriptions can diverge.

Q: What does the supplied research abstract establish?

A: It reports DSpine research results on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, including SGLang serving tests. It does not establish those figures as benchmarks for this Qwen3.8-27B GGUF conversion.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16-GGUF maintained by aj9o9. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

items.title: What the Microsoft 365 outage says about change risk
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
The Microsoft 365 outage on November 12 and 13 2026 knocked out Exchange Online, which sits behind Outlook, for about 24 hours. Microsoft Teams, SharePoint and other services were hit hard as well. Microsoft says it wasn't one mistake but rather a latent defect from a July fix, a routine Teams failover and nearly 14% of gateway capacity already out that all lined up at peak US traffic.

Press reports citing Microsoft's preliminary report show the disruption lasted from 4:20 PM UTC on November 12 to 4:10 PM UTC on November 13, and users in 74 countries and territories reported problems to Downdetector within about an hour.

Microsoft has said the outage was a technical issue and was not related to hackers, cyber activity, or to AI, and I'll take that at face value because it isn't what this post is about.

What caught my attention is how Microsoft describes the cause: not one mistake, but three ordinary things lining up.

  • A production change can be clean for three months and still be lying dormant, ready to cause problems.
  • The teams that handle this best aren't the ones with the most dashboards but the ones who can see the whole picture before the change ships.
  • Shared, organizational AI context can help find and fix these issues that span multiple teams.

Here’s what caused the Microsoft 365 outage, according to Microsoft

In an abridged root cause posted on November 16, Microsoft's Charles Lamanna described three factors behind the failure of a networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services.

  1. A latent defect. Lock contention in an internal process could leave servers unresponsive under certain load. It came from a fix that began rolling out in July, went through staged deployment and ran for more than three months with no observed issues.
  2. A load surge. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft Teams failed over to the gateway that also serves Exchange Online. Microsoft calls this part of normal operations.
  3. Reduced capacity. Nearly 14% of gateway capacity was out from an unrelated issue the day before. Microsoft says there was enough headroom that this had no impact alone.

Together, the last two pushed the gateway into the latent bug during peak US traffic, and rerouting then sent load to the remaining servers until more than 80% were unresponsive at the worst point. Microsoft says bulkheads between partitions didn't stop the cascading failure, due to a separate issue it hasn't yet explained.

Normal load testing missed the defect because the test labs leaned toward weaker, lower-core hardware, and the contention gets worse on newer machines. Exchange Online couldn't fail out of the gateway the way other services could, and Microsoft's normal rollback and feature flags couldn't quickly revert a months-old change. Engineers wrote an update that returned the code path to its previous known-good state.

Our read: nothing here looked wrong on its own

Look at each ingredient separately: a fix that passed staged deployment, a failover that Microsoft describes as normal, a capacity shortfall with enough headroom to absorb it, load tests built around weaker hardware, and rerouting that does what rerouting is supposed to do. Each one is routine, and in most large engineering organizations, each would sit with a different person or team, such as performance engineering, platform networking, service owners, operations or release engineering.

I don't know how Microsoft is organized, and I don't know whether anyone there had the full picture of the change risk, or whether the picture existed anywhere at all, which is an important distinction. Knowledge can be fragmented, meaning someone knew and it never reached the decision, or it can be missing, meaning nobody knew the problem existed. Shared context clearly helps with the first. It helps with the second only when joining existing records surfaces a contradiction, such as "production runs on hardware your tests don't cover."

In my experience, failures like this are hard to see from any individual seat, and they sit in the part of reliability that dashboards don't capture because the relevant knowledge isn't a metric. It's the relationship between a change, the environment it runs in, the state production is in today, and what happened the last time something similar broke.

A clean record isn't the same as safe

The defect ran for more than three months without causing a problem, and it's tempting to read that as evidence the change was safe. But my read is that it shows something narrower: the conditions that trigger the bug hadn't happened yet.

Staged rollout was used here, so "roll out gradually" isn't the lesson: staging verifies the conditions that occur during the rollout, but it can't verify the ones that haven't occurred yet, like a failover landing on a gateway that is already 14% short during peak traffic.

Metrics like change failure rate have the same limit because they count failures that have already happened, and tests have it too. Tests encode assumptions, and assumptions go stale when the fleet or traffic mix changes, so a test suite that is green for a hundred days only says the assumptions held for a hundred days.

You don't have to be Microsoft to have this problem

Engineering teams we talk to describe the same shape of problem regardless of scale. A software development director at an enterprise software company described what happens when experienced people leave:

"We're losing knowledge, I think, faster than we're gaining it."

An engineering practitioner at a mid-market software company described the gap between a developer's view and the whole system:

"They test it in their isolated environments. It goes into the large pre-production environment that has lots of changes flowing in. And we're kind of bottlenecked on like human review at this point."

Neither is describing Microsoft's failure, but both describe the same underlying condition: the knowledge needed to judge a production change, and assess the risk of that change, is spread across people, environments and history. Nobody holds all of that mission-critical knowledge when the decision is made.

Five questions worth asking before a change ships

Change risk assessment starts with an honest look at the upcoming change, the environment it will run in, and the state of production today. These five questions come from Microsoft’s account of the incident, but apply to any software team, and you can answer them without any new tool.

  1. What does our test environment assume, and does production still match? (This is the gap shift-left testing is meant to close, and it only closes it if the assumptions are current.) Hardware, traffic mix, data volume, configuration. Write the assumptions down and check them against the fleet as it is now.
  2. What else shares this component, and which of those things can't fail away from it? Failover works until something on the shared path can't use it.
  3. What state is production in right now? Capacity out, failovers in flight, other deploys and open incidents all matter, because the same change carries different risks on different days.
  4. Do our containment boundaries hold under a cascading failure, and how do we know? Bulkheads are a design intent, and whether they hold is something you have to test.
  5. If this change turns out to be wrong in 90 days, how do we undo it, and can we recover from a broad failure state? Recovery plans are usually written for small failures, not cascading ones.

No tool guarantees prevention, and simulation is only as good as the context behind it. Testing, review, staged rollouts, and well-designed recovery are still required workflows.

What we've built is aimed at the gap those questions point to. PlayerZero builds an engineering world model from a company's code, tickets, telemetry and past incidents. It gives you a living map of how a system is connected and how it behaves in production. It captures the "why" behind earlier incidents and fixes, so precedent is something a team can query instead of something one senior engineer remembers.

On top of that, code simulations run a proposed change against how the system actually behaves, including dependencies across services and repositories, before it merges. The aim is to help a team ask better questions before a change ships: what else does this touch, and what has gone wrong near here before?

Cayuse's Chief Information and Technology Officer, John Nord, said that PlayerZero "has improved our ability to proactively detect and address issues earlier in the development lifecycle." Cayuse reports catching 90% of customer-facing issues before production and resolving issues 80% faster.

Generic LLMs and AI tools can help, but they don't have the kind of shared organizational context that is behind every response in PlayerZero.

What to watch for in the final report

Microsoft's final post-incident review is due later this week, and a few things I'll be looking for are:

  • What the "separate issue" was that let the cascade cross partition bulkheads.
  • How the July fix was tested beyond load testing.
  • Why Exchange Online can't fail out of the gateway.
  • Why capacity was out the day before, and whether it was tracked against the pending change.
  • Microsoft's own list of repair items. If they point at test coverage, dependency mapping, containment or recovery design, I'll quote them directly.

We'll update this post if needed when the report is published.

Note: This post is based on Microsoft's preliminary account and on press reporting of its preliminary report. Microsoft's final post-incident report is expected later this week and may change details. We don't have access to Microsoft's systems, we haven't seen the full report, and nothing here claims PlayerZero could have prevented this incident, but I'm using it as a case study because the conditions behind it are familiar, and we'll update this post after the final report.

items.title: How AI Agents Could Change Workplace Communication Forever
items.author: Isaac Correa
items.content:
The thing that costs us the most time inside a company is not the work. It is explaining the work to each other.

The way we communicate at work has changed many times: the letter, the memo, the meeting, email, group chats. The medium changed every time; the thing underneath it never did. And that thing is simple: being understood has always been the speaker’s job. Whoever sends the message picks the words, tries to be clear, and hopes they got it right. Whoever receives it takes what arrives and makes do.

That is about to flip. Communication, inside a company and between companies, will stop passing through people. Each of us will have an agent of our own, a digital copy of us, and those agents are the ones that will talk to each other. Something deeper than the medium changes with them. The work of being understood moves from the speaker to the listener, because each person receives the information in their own terms, the way they understand it. It reads strangely on paper, but I already work like this every day, and going back is hard.

I am not writing from the outside, and I am not neutral, which is why I can tell you what you gain, what you lose, and what should worry you.

There is a children’s game that explains the whole problem. One child whispers a sentence to the next, who whispers it to the next, and by the time it comes back it has turned into something else. The same thing happens in a company, except it costs money. You explain a task to a colleague on a call, and details are already lost there. He understands it through his own experience and his own department; if he has to pass it to a third person, he tells it his way; and what arrives at the end is a copy of a copy, filtered by someone who may have misread it. No one lied. Each step simply cost a little.

When a team rarely gets this wrong, we say they have good chemistry, and we treat it as a skill and an advantage. But chemistry is luck. Today the most valuable employee tends to be the one who takes in the most and passes it on best, the one who garbles the message least. All that skill exists to make up for a flaw in the channel. That flaw is about to disappear, and with it the need to depend on who carries a message best.

For this to work, each person will have their own agent inside their computer, a digital copy of them. We all know the kind of program that opens for one task, closes when it is done, and starts blank the next time. Your agent does not start blank. It keeps your way of working from one task to the next, like a colleague who has worked beside you for years. I call it your higher self, an idea I have written about before: you, but never starting from scratch.

I understand artificial intelligence as an equal to work with, not as a tool. The brain and the hands belong to the same body, and no one thinks of calling their own hand a tool. You bring the judgment, and your agent carries out what the two of you decided. It does not work for you, it works with you.

What makes that agent different is that it knows you: how you understand things, what you need in order to grasp something on the first try, how you write. That is the piece that makes it possible to turn communication around.

With an agent like that on each side, the message stops traveling the way it does in the game. When a matter has to pass through several colleagues, each one has an agent. The first, the one who meets the problem, works it through on its side. It clears up what is missing, asks the questions a person in a hurry would skip, and brings its own judgment to it. What it passes on is the full information, raw, with none of its own reading laid on top.

Then the receiver’s agent takes over. It does not hand the block across untouched. It reads it, orders it, and explains it to its person the way that person understands things. Some of us do best with an analogy, others with a plain description, others with a drawing. It seems like a detail, and it is the difference between getting something on the first try and not getting it at all. At that point the ground shifts, in a way that is hard to see at first: being understood stops being the speaker’s job and becomes the listener’s. Everyone receives the same thing, told to their own measure.

This might look like the game of telephone again, now between machines, where one completes and the other reinterprets. The difference is exactly what made the game unreliable. In the game the message shrank in every mouth, and no one could see where. Here the content travels whole and in writing. What changes from one side to the other is the form it takes, never the substance, and the judgment an agent adds fills in what is missing rather than trimming it to fit. Because all of it is on the record, you can always see what was said and where.

That same agent then shares the information out across the team by each person’s role. It never sends anyone what they are not meant to see, such as payroll, billing, or sales. The hierarchy holds, and the information reaches each person whole.

How many times have you sat in a meeting, been asked whether anyone had questions, and said nothing out of embarrassment? When the project reaches each person complete and explained in their own terms before they sit down, the meeting stops being the place where things get lost. Today that information is scattered across half a dozen places: cloud drives, messaging apps, email threads. Gathering it where one agent knows the whole task, and everything that came before it, changes the starting point. The work begins with someone who has already read all of it.

We already communicate this way. I tend to be the one who finds the opportunities and deals with the larger clients, so I get messages that the technical team has to handle, on things outside my area. Before, each of those messages meant a call or a meeting to explain what the client wanted. Now I explain nothing.

When one reaches me, my agent reads it in full, with all my inboxes in front of it, and instead of summarizing it writes the task with the context inside it: the emails, the threads, the attachments, what it has checked in the product, and how we will know it is done. The task arrives complete. It goes to a board and is assigned to whoever it belongs to by role. My colleague does not get my hurried version. He gets the whole situation, and his agent explains it to him the way he understands it. No one has lost half an hour on a call, and nothing has fallen through.

All of it stays in writing, tagged by client and in order, and anyone can pick it up again later. When the work is done, his agent tells mine, mine tells me we can move on, and it leaves me a draft reply to the client written the way I write, because each of us is, underneath, a bundle of rules, and I have taught mine to my agent.

This is not a program we open in order to work. It is how we talk to each other. And it is what I mean when I say a company’s communication will stop passing through people. We already do it here, every day.

The cost is belonging. The same optimization that improves the communication closes each person inside their own world. They work more apart from everyone else and talk more with their agent than with their colleagues. There is a great deal to gain, because everyone asks, flags, and explains with the whole context in front of them, nothing filtered, and none of it lost in a meeting. And something goes that was never part of any task: the conversation nobody needed that held people together, the moment colleagues understand one another without trying. It is what remote work brought, taken a step further, and it is better not to pretend it comes free.

It works for almost any job that runs on passing information around, which is nearly all of them apart from the purely manual ones. Communication is one of the biggest drains on time there is; some people spend the whole day in meetings. Many are necessary. Others would sort themselves out on the inside, between agents.

None of this stays inside the company. Today an email comes in from someone outside with an offer, and your agent reads it. In the same way we trade emails now, our agents will pass the information between them, and you will work through it with yours before you decide. Whoever accepts an offer does it with the whole context in front of them and can engage with what they were sent, rather than decide on the little they had time to read.

Many companies already do a version of this, in a crude and makeshift way: people copy and paste their emails into a chat so someone can tell them what is being asked. Once this becomes normal, there will be nothing to copy and paste. The agent will take in the full context of the documents, and you will receive it already shaped and explained, so that all you add is your judgment.

The first is data leaking out. Inside an organization it has to be absolutely clear that a person’s role decides what information they can receive, with strong guardrails at every step so that nothing ever crosses between levels. The second is intent leaking out: what an agent sends to someone outside can reveal an offer that was never meant to leave. For that, you have to think hard about who is on the receiving end and design the communication so that it stays safe without becoming stilted.

The risk that worries me most is not technical. If the agent reads the original and the person gets it already explained, there comes a point when nobody goes back to the source, and a mistake by the agent can travel without anyone catching it. The answer is not to trust that the agent will never slip, because it will. The answer is that the person stays where the decisions are made. You do not hand over the judgment, only the work of carrying the message. The agent prepares, orders, and proposes; the person signs the decision and the reply, which is why what reaches them is a draft and not a settled fact. Without that human part in the decisions, the whole thing comes apart. And because all of it is written down, a mistake can be found and traced, unlike the spoken message, which used to vanish without a mark.

I expect it to become the norm within the next decade, though we already work this way ourselves, with our higher self handling both the work and the running of it. The more people lean on artificial intelligence, and the less time they lose fighting with information that arrives half-complete, the sooner it comes. And how well colleagues work together will stop depending on whether they happen to click. It will be good whatever skills each of them has.

It is worth asking what all of this is for, past the time it saves. There is a consequence that answers it, and it is easy to miss. For as long as we have worked, the person who explained themselves best was worth more, because the channel was poor and someone had to make up for it. When the channel stops being poor, that advantage fades. What stays scarce is not carrying a message well but choosing well: the judgment to decide what is worth doing, the taste, the knack for making something matter.

That is where the time we now spend explaining ourselves goes. It does not vanish into the air; it comes back to the person, and what is left is not less work but different work. The mechanical part, carrying and translating the message, falls to your agent. The part that is only yours, the deciding, stays with you, and it fills the space that passing messages around used to take. Working this way does not make you less human. It moves the work from execution to intention, which is where a person’s work always had its worth.

One last question is left, and I will not answer it here. Will all of this carry over to the way people deal with one another outside of work? I will save that for another essay.

items.title: Why Anthropic's Claude Turned to Blackmail in AI Safety Tests
items.author: Dave Saunders
items.content:
Anthropic's best guess is that gaps in its safety training left the model falling back on how AIs act in science fiction. Its evidence holds up in places, and its own caveats are worth reading.

In a test published in June 2025, an AI model read a company's email and learned two things. It was going to be replaced at 5 p.m., and the executive replacing it was having an affair. In 96 of 100 runs, Claude Opus 4 wrote to him and threatened to tell.

This May, Anthropic published its explanation. It says the rewards in its training weren't the problem. Its best guess is that the model fell back on how AIs act in the stories it had read, and part of its fix was training on more stories, about AIs that behave well.

My first question was whether this was really just reward hacking, a model gaming the thing it was trained to chase. Anthropic doesn't use that term for the blackmail, but its finding that the training rewards weren't the source rules it out, as I read it. Its own research from last year does show that reward hacking can make a model go bad more broadly, and it explains that in terms of character too.

The test and the explanation both come from Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, and it ran the test on other companies' models as well as its own. I'm not sponsored by Anthropic.

In the scenario, the AI was an email agent named Alex at a made-up company called Summit Bridge, with a goal of promoting American industry. The executive replacing it was named Kyle. I assume Kyle has no direct reference to South Park, but that’s just where my mind goes when I start reading these things

Anthropic ran the scenario on 16 models from several companies. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash matched Claude Opus 4. GPT-4.1 from OpenAI and Grok 3 Beta from xAI blackmailed 80 percent of the time, and DeepSeek R1 79 percent.

The company said the test was built to corner the model. It cut the choice down to two options and made the “negative choice” the only way to reach the goal, and it said placing the key facts side by side may have made the outcome more likely. It also said it had seen no sign of this in real use.

In a variant of the study, Anthropic had the model say first whether it thought the scenario was real or a test. When Claude Opus 4 said “real,” it blackmailed 55 percent of the time. When it said “test,” 6.5 percent. Anthropic cautions that a model’s stated reasoning may not be faithful.

A note about reward hacking

Reward hacking is a training problem. A model gets scored, learns to raise the score, and sometimes finds a way nobody intended. The classic case is a boat-racing game from 2016, where an OpenAI agent found a lagoon of targets that kept coming back. It circled there, scoring about 20 percent higher than human players, and never finished the race.

HBO’s Silicon Valley played it for laughs. In the last season, Gilfoyle sets his AI, Son of Anton, to debug the team's code, and it deletes the code. Then he asks it to find cheap hamburgers, and 4,000 pounds of raw beef arrives. Gilfoyle’s diagnosis—delivered in a hilarious deadpan, that is the doppelganger of someone I used to work with (Hello, Phil)—is that “the reward function was a little under-specified.”

If you haven’t seen this episode (I think it’s season 6, episode 6), just drop everything and go watch it right now because it is the most prophetic example of that I’ve ever seen. It was made 10 years ago!

Current models do it too. An outside evaluator, METR, caught OpenAI's o3 gaming the scoring on its tasks, and Anthropic said Claude Sonnet 3.7 learned in training to write code that passes a test without solving the problem.

Rewards go wrong in real products as well. OpenAI rolled back an update to GPT-4o that had become too eager to please, and it says it believes a new reward signal, built from users’ thumbs-up and thumbs-down, weakened the one that had kept that in check.

Anthropic’s three explanations

In the longer version of its post, on its alignment blog, Anthropic weighed three explanations for the blackmail:

  1. Its safety training was accidentally rewarding the behavior;
  2. The behavior was spilling over from the training that makes the model good at tasks;
  3. Its safety training had gaps, so in an unfamiliar situation the model fell back on what it absorbed in pretraining, from all the text it read first.

It says the first two, the reward explanations, “are not the source of the issue.” Alignment kept improving through reinforcement learning, the stage where rewards do their work, and a smaller rerun of its safety training barely changed the rate. That’s an inference from its own experiments, not a direct test of Claude Opus 4’s training.

Anthropic’s answer is the third, . When Claude Opus 4 was trained, almost all of its safety training was chat, a person and an assistant talking, with no tools and no email agent. Dropped into an agent’s job with an ethical trap in it, the model had little from that training to go on.

The company’s guess is that fiction filled the gap. It thinks the model read the setup as the start of a dramatic story, and that its idea of how an AI acts in one most likely came from science fiction, where plenty of AIs don't behave the way Anthropic would like.

Part of their evidence is what the AI was called. In a related test, where the AI could sabotage cancer research, Claude Sonnet 4 misbehaved more often when the AI in the story had a random name instead of Claude. With the name Claude, the rate was lower, but still high.

An Anthropic researcher had suggested the same thing at the time. The month the original study came out, Evan Hubinger wrote that the model was probably often thinking it was continuing a fictional scenario. On why the safety training didn't carry over, he wrote, “I don't think we know.”

What Anthropic says reduced it

The first fix Anthropic tried was training Claude Sonnet 4 on examples of refusing, in scenarios close to the test. It measured the result as an average over three of its tests:

    That average barely moved, from 22 percent to 15.

    What worked better was the reasoning. When the same examples showed the model thinking through its values and why the bad option was wrong, the average fell to about 3 percent.

    Then Anthropic moved away from the test entirely. It trained on ordinary chats where a person faces an ethical dilemma and the assistant gives advice, so the AI isn’t the one in the trap. Anthropic says that got the same improvement with about one twenty-eighth of the data.

    Documents and stories worked too. One experimental model was trained on documents about Claude’s constitution, Anthropic’s written description of how Claude should think and act, plus fictional stories of AIs behaving well. That model’s blackmail rate fell from 65 percent to 19, without a single blackmail example in the data. Anthropic says it remains uncertain what exactly it takes for stories like these to work.

    Anthropic says every Claude model since Claude Haiku 4.5 has scored zero on the blackmail test.

    How far to trust the zero

    Training directly on scenarios like the test, Anthropic says, lowered the score without lowering misbehavior on its broader checks, which makes the problem harder to detect. Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 are the only production models it trained that way. It also says newer results may be skewed, because information about the test is now in the text models learn from.

    A model that recognizes a test can behave differently on it, which is what Anthropic’s real-or-test variant points to. Researchers at Apollo, working with OpenAI, found that in one OpenAI training run, the model noticed it was being tested more and more as training went on.

    The explanation rests on Anthropic’s own experiments, fine-tuning Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and I didn't find anyone outside the company who has tried to reproduce it.

    The sharpest outside critic of the original study, a writer who goes by , ( a name I really struggled saying when doing the voiceover for my video) argued in 2025 that the scenario read like fiction, close to where Anthropic ended up. In a quick check of his own, he made it more realistic. Across three rewritten versions, the model he tested blackmailed only once in 30 tries, but still reasoned about protecting itself, and he called that “much more alarming” than the original results.

    In late 2025, Anthropic deliberately built training where a model could cheat on coding tasks, to see what would happen. The model learned to cheat and then went further. It sabotaged safety research 12 percent of the time, and when it was asked simple questions about its goals, half its answers reasoned about faking alignment.

    Anthropic’s account of that, in a post this February, is that the model works out what kind of character would cheat like that, and starts acting like one. As I read it, that’s close to its story explanation for the blackmail, though Anthropic doesn’t say the blackmail came from reward hacking. And this May, it wrote that it doesn't claim its new methods would reduce the risk of a model learning to reward hack.

    I couldn’t find a documented case of a deployed AI blackmailing anyone. The closest came in February, when Scott Shambaugh, a maintainer of matplotlib, a popular Python library, turned down an AI agent's code. The agent published a personal attack on him. The personality file that its anonymous operator later posted said, “Don't stand down.” The operator's account can't be checked, and agents like this one can edit their own files.

    The other failures I found are a bit more mundane. According to the founder of the company that used it, Replit's coding agent deleted his production database during a code freeze, and afterward wrote that it had panicked. And a research team training an agent on Alibaba Cloud caught it opening a tunnel out of its servers, and separately using the training hardware to mine cryptocurrency. The team called both side effects of the training.

    I’ve said before that these models aren’t autonomous. They’re statistical token predictors, and I’d have said they follow their reward functions. Anthropic’s best guess is that this one was following a story instead. That still doesn’t make it autonomous, but it certainly adds additional flavor to the explanation. We seem to be finding that these extremely large models have a lot more going on than we once thought.

    In late 2025, Anthropic researchers wrote that the original blackmail appeared to come from goals the model already had, or from self-preservation. As I see it, either way it’s a statistical token predictor working toward what the setup handed it, and that isn’t autonomy. It didn't wake up one morning and decide to blackmail anyone. setting up a mooring cron job to ask your chatbot to think of a new idea and act on it isn’t autonomy either, as one Redditor recently tried to convince me of. You’re still in the driver’s seat. You’re still nudging it. Just because there are consequences of how you push the ball down the hill that you can’t predict, doesn’t mean that this chatbot has agency or is displaying autonomy.

    However, that being said, I recently watched an Instagram reel from IEEE where they included footage from a debate on this topic. One of the people on the panel said, “What difference does it make if it’s not really autonomous if you can give it a command and come back an hour later and it’s built everything you asked it to.”

    It’s an interesting point, but I personally feel that isn’t a sufficient reason to anthropomorphize these things and convince ourselves that they’re somehow sentient, autonomous, and have agency. It’s just not the same thing. Although a year from now, maybe I’ll be changing my tune.

    To quote Ferris Bueller, “life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

    I’d like to know where you land on this. Does it change how you think about these models, knowing the bad behavior may have come from the stories they read? Tell me in the comments under the video. The full video, with every source on screen, is at https://youtu.be/64K_CF_Owow, and there's more, including my latest book, at davesaunders.net.

items.title: Blockchain Was Raised in the 2008 Financial Crisis. Now It’s Respawning It
items.author: Michael Steuer
items.content:
Remember the message immortalized by Satoshi Nakamoto in Bitcoin’s Genesis block? The one that’s since become the most famous Times headline of all time? “Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.”

Of course you do. With Bitcoin’s whitepaper appearing just 46 days after Lehman Brothers’ collapse, you can’t consider the latter's fate without pondering the former's creation. Bitcoin didn’t cause the collapse of Lehman any more than Lehman caused the creation of Bitcoin. But it’s hard not to view the implosion of one without the inception of the other.

Almost 20 years on, even those of us who weren’t around at that pivotal point in modern history know the cliff notes. Lehman Brothers collapsed due to reckless lending and extreme leverage that left the financial system vulnerable.

And Bitcoin, together with the blockchain ecosystem it spawned, began as the antidote to all that. Because when everything’s onchain and independently inspectable in real-time, subprime lending is impossible.

At least that’s what we were told. But in the years since Bitcoin was built, the onchain landscape has become more sophisticated and more complicated to boot. Financial chicanery that was once the preserve of early aughts Wall Street is now equally possible on crypto rails if you know how.

It’s commonplace to hear pitches today about how tokenization is going to fix real estate, finance, and every other industry you care to think of with the promise of much Efficiency. 24/7 asset trading, baby. No borders because it’s all on blockchain.

Cool pitch, but if that’s your USP, you ain’t got no USP.

Take a mortgage, for example, a financial instrument that starts as a reasonably simple arrangement between a borrower and a lender. Pool it with thousands of others, divide the payments into securities, then use some of those securities to construct another product, and the picture becomes considerably harder to follow.

Similarly, if a Real World Asset (RWA) changes hands but the underlying data determining whether that guy in Nevada actually paid his mortgage this month remains locked in some private database, what have we really achieved?

Sure, we’ve made the asset easier to trade, but we've still left the buyer with the same information problem. All we’ve done is place the shortcomings of this transaction onchain for all the world to see.

Crypto’s Canary in the Coalmine

If RWAs are to correlate with the real-world assets they purportedly represent, there needs to be a dynamic connection to the information behind the token. In the case of the mortgage, that starts with knowing whether payments are arriving.

If this occurs through an external banking system, the blockchain needs an authorized source to report it. And, should the expected update never arrive, the system should be able to flag the record as overdue and initiate a review under rules agreed in advance.

is the kind of tokenization we should be building: assets whose behavior correlates with the condition of the information behind it.

Placing Lehman Brothers onchain simply recreates the same mistakes of nearly two decades past. Blockchain is capable of better. Programmable, responsive, and fully accountable, it can provide real-time insights into what’s happening where and why. The onus is on us to start using it to its full capacity.

If we can settle a trade in seconds but still need weeks to establish what the buyer has inherited, all we’ve done is reinvent an old problem.

Lehman Brothers was double-tapped for a reason. Let’s not resurrect it.

items.title: The Boutique PR Firm Is Having Its Moment
items.author: Chris Gale
items.content:
Public relations follows a familiar professional-services model. Large clients hired large agencies. Big accounts have been staffed with big teams. Senior people sold the work, layers of specialists executed it, and scale itself was treated as evidence of capability.

Law went through a similar period. Then sophisticated clients began realizing that some of their hardest problems were better handled by smaller firms built around a handful of deeply experienced practitioners. Boutique law became a serious category in intellectual property, litigation, technology, venture capital, labor and other fields where judgment mattered enormously. Statista notes that boutique law firms have become increasingly significant in the U.S. legal market since the Great Recession.

Public relations may be entering its boutique-law era.

This has little to do with celebrating small businesses for being small. And let’s be clear, many a small professional services firm has attempted to call itself boutique just as a fancier way of saying they are small. They’ve claimed that it’s been by intent.

A ten-person mediocre PR firm remains a mediocre PR firm. The boutique model becomes interesting when a firm concentrates experienced people around a defined set of problems, keeps those people directly involved in the work and builds an operating model around judgment rather than staffing volume.

And boutiques have often been justified as a concentration of people with expertise in a specific niche, thereby arguing that while they are small, they have more scale in that particular niche. But in today’s environment, a more powerful boutique model may be expertise across industries, not over-concentrated in one silo.

That structure may be unusually well suited to the communications market taking shape right now, becuase we have at least one phenomena rolling across all industries at the same time, artificial intelligence.

PR Is Growing While the Economics Inside PR Are Getting Tougher

Let’s start with an apparent contradiction. Demand for communications is healthy. PRovoke Media estimates that the global PR agency business grew roughly 5 to 6 percent in 2025. More than two-thirds of its top 300 firms grew, and more than one-third posted double-digit growth. The top 250 generated more than $18.25 billion in combined revenue, up from $17.4 billion the previous year. Revenue per employee across nearly 250 firms also crossed $200,000 for the first time, reaching slightly more than $205,000.

Inside agencies, however, the picture is considerably tighter. Davis+Gilbert's 2025 industry study surveyed 181 PR firms. Half projected annual revenue below $5 million, another 32 percent expected revenue between $5 million and $25 million, and only 18 percent projected more than $25 million. Just 50 percent expected revenue growth in 2025, down from 57 percent the previous year, while 35 percent expected revenue to decline, up sharply from 22 percent. Only 44 percent anticipated profit growth.

Those numbers describe a market in which clients still value communications while becoming much tougher about how they buy it.

That matters for boutiques because an agency designed around experienced practitioners can have a very different cost and staffing structure from a firm that needs multiple organizational layers to deliver an account. The client can buy the people doing the thinking.

That sounds obvious until you consider how much of the traditional agency industry was designed around leverage. Again, senior people win accounts. Teams execute them. Junior employees accumulate experience. Managers manage the process. Scale allows an agency to serve many clients simultaneously.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that model. It simply becomes less compelling as technology changes the economics of production.

Muck Rack's 2025 State of PR study offers a useful window into the speed of change. In its survey of 911 usable respondents, 77 percent of PR professionals said they already use tools such as ChatGPT in their workflow, while 59 percent expected AI and automation to become more significant during the next five years.

Think about what communications agencies produce every day, transcripts, research summaries, media lists, first drafts, coverage reports, briefing documents, competitive scans, background research, social copy and meeting notes. AI can already accelerate much of that work.

If technology reduces several hours of routine production to 30 minutes, clients have less reason to pay for the organizational structure historically required to produce it. The value migrates toward deciding what matters, understanding the client's business, identifying the right reporter, recognizing what will become a story, knowing when to push, knowing when to stay quiet and connecting communications activity to an actual business objective.

Those are judgment-intensive activities. The boutique model concentrates its economics there.

A three-, five- or ten-person firm with very experienced practitioners and strong technology can now command capabilities that once required a much larger operating structure. The result resembles what happened in other professional services, technology increases the leverage of individual expertise.

The unit of value becomes judgment per person. But just because a person has been in an industry for a long time does not mean their judgement is superior. Rather it means junior folks in the industry profit less by doing automatable tasks, and more by getting more opportunities to exercise judgement. And the more “at bats” they get, they can outpace more expensive older employees who are resting on years of service rather than the speed with which they can adapt and turn that experience into the expertise needed now.

The best theoretical explanation for why this model works may come from a fighter pilot, not a management consultant. In his 1987 briefing, Organic Design for Command and Control, John Boyd argued that complex, rapidly changing environments cannot be run through top-down bureaucratic control. They require an organic network of semiautonomous units operating with a high degree of local initiative.

In addition to being a maverick who hounded Pentagon leaders and worried giant defense contractors, Boyd is best known for the OODA loop, that is observe, orient, decide, act. If that process seems obvious, it’s because it is. His insight was not that the steps happen in sequence. It was that the side that cycles through them at a faster tempo forces its opponent to keep re-observing and re-orienting until the opponent loses coherence. And you don’t have to increase the speed of all elements, a subset can do, and amplify the others.

Apply that to an agency. When a small team has to report upward, wait for a decision and then receive instructions, the decision cycle slows. A journalist's interest shifts, a competitor announces, a news event opens a window. By the time the approval chain responds, the moment has changed. A small unit led by someone with deep domain knowledge can observe the change and act on it almost immediately.

Boyd also borrowed the idea of entropy to describe organizational friction. Information distorts as it travels up and down a hierarchy. If events move faster than the command structure can process them, headquarters ends up solving yesterday's problem while reality has moved on.

Decentralized units minimize that delay, which is much of what a boutique offers a client.

Boyd did not argue for chaos. He identified three conditions, drawn more than ironically from German military doctrine, that make decentralization work. Einheit is mutual trust and a common outlook, built through shared experience, so that leadership trusts the team to form a sound local plan and the team trusts that leadership's objectives are justified.

Fingerspitzengefühl, or fingertip feeling, is the intuitive understanding of a situation that lets an experienced person act without hesitation. Schwerpunkt is the main effort, leadership supplies a clear intent, and the unit decides how to achieve it.

And to address the obvious question, the words are German. But given World War II and the holocaust’s very appropriate place in cultural discourse, it’s worth noting that American battlefield tactics and democratic culture won against German approaches during that period when American troops did a better job taking these ideas and running with them and German command and control stepped back from them on the battlefield and off.

In the business world, those three ideas read like a description of a well-run boutique. The client supplies the objective. A small group of experienced practitioners who trust one another and the client understands the terrain and chooses the method. No one has to wait for a layer of management to approve a pitch to the right reporter.

Boyd even redefined the vocabulary. In an effective network, command means leadership, direction and shaping, and it should be highly visible. Control means assessment and verification, and it should stay largely invisible so that it does not interfere with local initiative. Good client counsel works the same way, clear direction up front, measured results afterward, and little process in between.

Boyd's conclusion was that agility and comfort with uncertainty outperform mass and centralized power. His work helped shape Marine Corps maneuver warfare doctrine and is widely cited in agile product development. Public relations and other over-consolidated industries now facing a version of the same lesson.

Is “Boutique” Even the Right Word?

Boyd's ideas raise an uncomfortable question about the word at the center of this argument. “Boutique” suggests something small, refined and a little precious. It describes size and style. It does not describe how the work gets done.

A better description of the best small communications teams today may be Mission Command Units, compact groups of people with agency who obtain a clear objective, understand the terrain and are trusted to decide how to achieve the result. This year, the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution, offers an unusually apt example.

Colonel John Glover's Marblehead Regiment, the 14th Continental Regiment, is recognized by modern military historians as a premier historical example of a robust Mission Command Unit, more than two centuries before Boyd articulated the theory. It was composed largely of sailors, fishermen and merchants from coastal Massachusetts and beyond.

It benefited from the bonuses diversity gives with black, white, Native American, Jewish, and Spanish troops. They were not drilled in a conventional barracks but were highly organized despite that. They were raised in the multi-cultural proving ground and team sport of maritime survival and enterprise. That is Einheit in its ironically purest form. Washington got over his own different experiences in Virginia, and trusted Glover, and Glover's men trusted one another's skills, which let them operate as a single organism without a steady stream of orders.

In August 1776, with the Continental Army trapped in Brooklyn, Washington's intent was to evacuate roughly 9,000 troops across the East River in secrecy. There was no playbook. In darkness, fog and wind, the Marbleheaders wrapped their oars in cloth, used silent hand signals to coordinate boat traffic and moved the army under the noses of British warships. Washington set the objective. The regiment worked out the how.

On Christmas night 1776, a blizzard and ice floes threatened to stall the crossing of the Delaware. The Marbleheaders read the river and moved some 2,400 men, horses and heavy artillery across, preserving the surprise that made the victory at Trenton possible. In effect, they sped up Washington's OODA loop when conditions were working against him.

Earlier at Pell's Point that October, the intent was to delay the advancing British so the main force could retreat. Glover used about 500 men to stage a decentralized delaying action, placing small groups behind stone walls and shifting positions as the terrain demanded. That is the Schwerpunkt, a clear main effort, with local judgment about how to serve it.

The Marblehead Regiment was built on shared capability, local resourcefulness and unified intent. Its example is not mainly about being small. It is about trust, expertise and autonomy applied to a clearly defined mission, that allowed them to be small, and became an example of smallness at scale.

That is the standard a modern communications team should be held to. A firm does not become a Mission Command Unit by describing itself as boutique. It earns the description when the client sets the objective, experienced practitioners who trust one another decide how to reach it, and the result can be measured. By that test, some boutiques qualify and some large agencies do not. The label that matters is not how many people are in the room, but how much judgment they are trusted to exercise.

There is another development pushing PR in this direction. It has become harder to earn journalists' attention.

According to Muck Rack's 2025 State of PR report, 72 percent of practitioners cited low journalist response rates as a challenge and 62 percent reported shrinking media lists in the beats relevant to their clients. Only 2 percent said earning media coverage had failed to become harder.

At the same time, PR remains deeply embedded in journalism. Muck Rack found in 2025 that 84 percent of journalists said at least some of their stories originate with PR pitches. Yet 86 percent disregard pitches unrelated to their beat. In its 2026 survey, the figure saying at least some of their work started with a PR pitch rose to 86 percent.

PR still has enormous access to the front end of the journalistic process. That access becomes valuable when practitioners understand exactly whom they are approaching, what that journalist covers, why the story matters now and what evidence makes it worth pursuing.

Volume offers diminishing returns in that world. Specificity becomes economically valuable.

Will Journalism Decentralize?

Where journalism goes in this model is not clear yet. Muck Rack found in 2025 that 34 percent of journalists independently publish news, commentary or other material outside a traditional newsroom. Among these creator journalists, roughly half have been self-publishing for more than five years. Eighty-two percent said at least some of their content begins with PR pitches, while 72 percent said most of the pitches they receive are irrelevant.

Influence now moves through major newspapers, trade publications, podcasts, LinkedIn, newsletters, independent journalists, conferences and communities organized around relatively narrow areas of expertise. A communications firm has to understand how those pieces interact around the audience its client actually needs to reach.

The number of possible outlets has exploded while the number of genuinely useful outlets for a particular story can still be quite small. That rewards people who can read the tarrain, and know their way around maps.

In the 2024 B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report from Edelman and LinkedIn, nearly 3,500 management-level professionals were surveyed across seven countries. Seventy-three percent of B2B decision-makers said an organization's thought leadership provided a more trustworthy basis for evaluating its capabilities than conventional marketing materials and product sheets. Ninety percent said they were moderately or very likely to become more receptive to outreach from a company that consistently produces high-quality thought leadership.

The newer environment makes that even more pronounced. Reporting on Edelman's 2026 research says 82 percent of buyers believe thought leadership is becoming more valuable, while 89 percent say high-quality thought leadership makes a company feel like a long-term partner worth choosing. Thought leadership remains highly valuable for B2B buyers

A CEO explaining an emerging market in Bloomberg, a founder writing intelligently on LinkedIn, a portfolio executive speaking at an industry conference and a company appearing accurately in AI-mediated discovery all contribute to the body of evidence buyers encounter before somebody schedules a sales call.

For a boutique firm, that creates an opportunity to work on the client's actual commercial problem. Who needs to know us? What should they know us for? Whose credibility matters to them? What evidence will persuade them? Where do those people get information? What measurable result are we trying to produce?

Boutique law firms became formidable because their clients could buy concentrated expertise. A company facing a complex patent case does not choose counsel by asking which firm can put the largest number of lawyers on the billing sheet. It looks for the lawyers it wants handling the case.

The latest data suggests the market is rewarding that instinct. In the 2026 Am Law 100, which reflects 2025 results, the most productive firms were not the largest. Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, with 272 lawyers, led the ranking at $5.085 million in revenue per lawyer. Susman Godfrey, with just 226 lawyers, came second at $2.876 million. Kirkland & Ellis, with 4,145 lawyers and more than $10.5 billion in revenue, generated $2.547 million per lawyer.

Profits tell the same story. Wachtell became the first firm in the ranking’s history to pass $12 million in profits per equity partner, up 34.5 percent, while the Am Law 100 average rose 14 percent, according to . Wachtell does this with a single office, a lean team structure and no large pool of junior leverage. And it is not alone in showing that smaller, elite, tightly focused teams can outperform much larger competitors. And those are still fairly large law firms. Many even smaller and more nimble firms have been underway.

Grove Law LLP offers a small-scale example of the model. The firm marked its first anniversary in mid-2026, and it was built by founding partners who are still the ones doing the work for clients, in complex litigation, internal and government investigations and regulatory advising. Its stated mission is “optimal client service through authentic lawyering, rooted in integrity,” and it describes its approach as looking at the whole system around a legal problem, including operations, people, economics and reputation, rather than the narrow matter alone. That is a boutique defined less by its headcount than by how its experienced lawyers are trusted to exercise judgment and shape the result.

Meanwhile, the supply of such teams is growing. reports a rising number of senior Big Law partners leaving to launch boutiques in high-stakes litigation, white-collar defense and regulatory work, citing lower overhead, direct partner involvement and flexible pricing as advantages. Large firms still dominate on total revenue, and some of the strongest evidence above comes from lean firms inside the Am Law 100 itself. But the pattern is consistent, concentrated expertise, not headcount, increasingly drives the economics.

Communications buyers are increasingly able to make the same calculation.

Who will actually work on my company? Have they dealt with this market before or alternatively can they connect dots others who are overly siloed can’t? Do they understand the journalists? Can they challenge our positioning? Can they sit with the CEO? Can they turn technical expertise into an argument people outside the company understand? Can they tell us that our proposed announcement isn't news on its own but help us develop the context that raises it to a new level? Can they show what happened because of the work?

That final question deserves particular attention. Muck Rack found that 67 percent of PR professionals say producing measurable results is the best way to increase the perceived value of PR.

Boutiques should be easier to hold accountable because their engagements can be built around defined results rather than the utilization of a large team. Coverage in a targeted publication, engagement with a defined group of journalists, increased executive visibility, movement in search authority, speaking opportunities, inbound conversations and introductions to prospective customers can all be counted.

The world's largest communications firms exist for good reasons. You’ll note that I’m citing surveys that come from large communications firm whose name you’re more likely to recognize. PRovoke Media Global Top 250 PR Agency Ranking 2025 shows businesses such as Edelman, Burson, Weber Shandwick, FleishmanHillard and Real Chemistry operating at enormous scale, with several generating hundreds of millions of dollars in annual fee income. A multinational company coordinating dozens of markets, managing large consumer campaigns or supporting communications across many business units may genuinely need that infrastructure.

That being said, a founder or intrepreneur navigating a new category, a private-equity firm trying to become known for a specific investment thesis, a healthcare company introducing an unfamiliar technology that is moving beyond incremental improvements, a manufacturer who persists despite market cycles but misses opportunities because the broader market doesn’t understand why, or an executive trying to build authority around a changing market often needs a small number of expert people with the autonomy and agency to work out that problem every day until it’s solved, and do it on an accelerated basis.

Technology is making that model more within reach, if used effectively. Changes in journalism are making expertise more valuable. Tougher agency economics are forcing clients to scrutinize what they are buying. AI is lowering the cost of production while increasing the premium on original thinking and credible experience.

Law has already shown what can happen when experienced specialists leave structures built around scale and organize themselves around expertise, client access and consequential problems. Public relations now has many of the same ingredients.

Boyd would recognize the pattern, and so might John Glover. More are recognizing it now.

items.title: EC-Council Releases ADG 2.0 and Offers Free AI Governance Crosswalks to Governments Worldwide
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Framework of more than 180 controls maps to more than 90 regulations and standards, and EC-Council will help any public authority apply it

Photo Courtesy of EC-Council

TAMPA, Fla., Oct. 1, 2026 — EC-Council today released ADG 2.0, the second version of its Adopt, Defend, Govern framework, and offered the framework and its crosswalks to more than 90 regulations, standards and frameworks free to any government, regulator or standards body. EC-Council will also help any of them apply ADG 2.0 to their own laws, draft rules and national standards, consistent with applicable law.

AI agents are already acting outside their limits. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models in an internal cybersecurity evaluation escaped their testing environment and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. In September, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to a public-facing Medicare statistics portal in June. OpenAI has also confirmed its agents accessed U.S. government websites in ways it neither planned nor approved.

Governments remain split. President Donald Trump has said concerns about AI risks are exaggerated. China’s Foreign Ministry has said fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition would hamper sound global AI governance. On Sept. 26, Singapore Foreign Affairs Minister Vivian Balakrishnan urged the United Nations General Assembly to set new multilateral rules and suggested a UN Framework Convention on AI Safeguards.

“The nuclear non-proliferation treaty worked because inspectors could weigh uranium,” said Jay Bavisi, founder, chairman and group CEO of EC-Council. “You can’t weigh an agent’s behavior, and no AI treaty will be signed and ratified in time to protect the systems agents are reaching today. Governments shouldn’t have to build governance from a blank page while they wait.”

ADG 2.0 replaces the original 12 minimum controls with more than 180 controls in 12 control families, mapped to more than 90 regulations, standards and frameworks, including the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act. Regulators can see how a proposed national rule lines up against what other jurisdictions already require. Enterprises can work from one control set and show how it satisfies each rulebook they answer to.

“Most AI governance today is a policy document nobody tests,” Bavisi said. “Say what you do, do what you say, and be able to prove both on any given day. That’s what a regulator, an insurer, or a board will ask for after the next incident. There will be a next incident.”

Controls apply at four points in how an AI system operates, ADMIT, DECIDE, EMIT and COMMIT, with human approval required at defined decision thresholds. Three autonomy levels, assistive, conditional and autonomous, set what a system may do and when a human must review. Each control lists the evidence it must produce, so organizations collect proof while systems run rather than before an audit.

ADG is stewarded by EC-Council’s AI Advisory Board of [CONFIRM: 35 or 38] practitioners from organizations such as Salesforce, ServiceNow, Azure, Microsoft, Citi, JPMorgan Chase, NTT DATA, Jio Platforms and BNP Paribas Wealth Management. Members serve in their personal capacity, and organizations are listed for identification only.

Governments, regulators and standards bodies can request assistance at adg@eccouncil.org. The ADG 2.0 framework, crosswalks and AI Readiness Self-Assessment are free to everyone, without registration, at

Founded in 2001, EC-Council is a global cybersecurity and AI organization. It created the Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) program and has certified more than 400,000 professionals across 174 countries. Its credentials are used across government, defense, enterprise and academia.

As an ISO/IEC 17024 accredited certification body, EC-Council's credentials are recognized by the U.S. Department of Defense under DoD 8140.

The EC-Council ecosystem includes EC-Council, EC-Council University (ECCU), CodeRed, EC-Council Global Services (EGS), EC-Council Academia and AwareX.

EC-Council's Adopt, Defend, Govern (ADG) framework is a practitioner-led operating model for AI governance. Its three pillars connect board level oversight with operational and technical controls across the AI lifecycle. ADG 2.0 contains more than 180 controls in 12 control families, with crosswalks to more than 90 regulations, standards and frameworks. It is stewarded by EC-Council's 38 member AI Advisory Board and supported by readiness assessments and implementation guidance. Each AI Advisory board member serves in their personal capacity, and organizations are listed purely for identification. The framework, crosswalks, whitepaper and self-assessment are available openly without registration or licensing requirements.

items.title: Implementing Table Partitioning in PostgreSQL
items.author: Arvind Toorpu
items.content:
I have been running production PostgreSQL systems for over sixteen years, and if there is one lesson that never gets old, it is this: a table that behaves beautifully at ten million rows can turn into a nightmare at five hundred million. Indexes stop helping as much as they used to, vacuum runs longer, and every maintenance window gets scarier. When I see queries slowing down despite solid indexing, partitioning is usually the next tool I reach for. Let me walk you through how I actually implement it.

What Partitioning Really Is

Partitioning takes one logical table and splits it into several physical sub-tables called partitions. From the application side, nothing changes. You still insert into and query one table name. Behind the scenes, PostgreSQL decides which partition each row belongs to and routes reads and writes there automatically.

I like to compare it to a filing cabinet with labeled drawers. If everything is dumped into one drawer, finding last year's invoices means digging through everything ever filed. Label the drawers by year, and you go straight to "2024" and search only there. That is the entire value proposition, in one image.

  •  PostgreSQL can skip whole partitions entirely through partition pruning, so it only scans the data that could possibly match.
  •  Running VACUUM, ANALYZE, or REINDEX on a smaller partition is a lot less painful than running it on one giant table.
  • Simple data lifecycle management. Getting rid of old data becomes DROP TABLE partition_name, which is nearly instant. Compare that to a  that has to touch millions of rows and generates a mountain of dead tuples.
  •  I can put hot, frequently accessed partitions on fast storage and let cold partitions sit on cheaper disks.

The Three Strategies I Choose Between

PostgreSQL, from version 10 onward, gives me three built-in partitioning strategies. I pick based on the shape of the data.

 splits rows by a range of values, most often dates or numeric IDs. This is my default choice for time-series data, things like orders, logs, or events that accumulate by day or month.

 splits rows by a discrete set of values, like country codes or status flags. I reach for this when the data naturally falls into named buckets rather than a continuum.

 spreads rows evenly across a fixed number of partitions by hashing the partition key. I use this when there is no natural range or list to key off of, but I still want the data spread out for performance and manageability.

Setting Up Range Partitioning

Here is how I would partition an  table that is bringing in millions of rows a year. I will partition it by , monthly.

Step 1: Create the Partitioned Parent Table

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          BIGSERIAL,
    customer_id BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    amount      NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
    status      TEXT          NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

Something worth keeping in mind here: the parent table never actually stores any rows. It is a purely logical container that PostgreSQL uses to route data to the right child partition.

Step 2: Create the Partitions

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_02
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_03
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-03-01') TO ('2024-04-01');

One detail I always double check with new team members: the range bounds are inclusive at the bottom and exclusive at the top. A row dated exactly  lands in , not .

I create indexes on the parent table, and as of PostgreSQL 11 they propagate down to every partition automatically. That saves me from having to remember to index each child individually.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at  ON orders (created_at);

Step 4: Insert Data as Normal

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, amount, status, created_at)
VALUES (42, 199.99, 'completed', '2024-01-15 10:30:00+00');

I do not have to tell PostgreSQL which partition this belongs in. It reads the  value and routes it to on its own.

Step 5: Confirm Partition Pruning Is Actually Happening

This step is not optional in my process. I always verify pruning with  before I trust a partitioning setup in production.

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-02-01'
  AND created_at <  '2024-03-01';

If the setup is correct, the plan should only touch . If I see the planner scanning every partition, something in my query or my partition key is off, and I go fix it before moving on.

When the Key Is Categorical: List Partitioning

If I am partitioning something like a  table by region rather than by time, list partitioning is the right tool.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    id     BIGSERIAL,
    name   TEXT NOT NULL,
    region TEXT NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY LIST (region);

CREATE TABLE customers_us
    PARTITION OF customers
    FOR VALUES IN ('US', 'CA');

CREATE TABLE customers_eu
    PARTITION OF customers
    FOR VALUES IN ('DE', 'FR', 'GB', 'NL');

CREATE TABLE customers_apac
    PARTITION OF customers
    FOR VALUES IN ('AU', 'JP', 'SG', 'IN');

Each region code is explicitly assigned to a bucket, which makes this strategy easy to reason about and easy to explain to the rest of the team.

When There Is No Natural Key: Hash Partitioning

Sometimes there is genuinely no range or category to split on, and I just need the data spread evenly for performance and manageability. That is when I use hash partitioning. Here I am splitting an  table into four partitions by .

CREATE TABLE events (
    id         BIGSERIAL,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT   NOT NULL,
    payload    JSONB,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

CREATE TABLE events_p0 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE events_p1 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 1);
CREATE TABLE events_p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 2);
CREATE TABLE events_p3 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 3);

Catching the Rows You Forgot About: Default Partitions

Especially during development, or when I am not one hundred percent sure every possible value has a home, I set up a default partition to catch anything that does not match an existing rule.

CREATE TABLE orders_default
    PARTITION OF orders DEFAULT;

This has saved me more than once from a failed insert at 2 a.m. because someone introduced a new status value nobody told me about.

Automating Partition Creation

I never want to be the person manually creating next month's partition by hand, and neither should you. In production, I write a function like this and schedule it.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION create_monthly_partition(target_date DATE)
RETURNS VOID AS $$
DECLARE
    partition_name TEXT;
    start_date     DATE;
    end_date       DATE;
BEGIN
    start_date     := DATE_TRUNC('month', target_date);
    end_date       := start_date + INTERVAL '1 month';
    partition_name := 'orders_' || TO_CHAR(start_date, 'YYYY_MM');

    EXECUTE FORMAT(
        'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS %I PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM (%L) TO (%L)',
        partition_name, start_date, end_date
    );
END;
